drugs.indications: Fungal nail infections
drugs.dosages: Apply to affected nail once or sometimes twice a week after filling and cleansing, allow to dry, treat finger nail for 6 months, toe nail for 9-12 months (review at intervals of 3 months)
drugs.adverseReactions: Slight transient burning sensation
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to amorolfine
drugs.interactions: Not known
drugs.precautions: Avoid contact with eyes, previous hypersensitivity or intolerance to other topical antifungal agents
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Used for superficial and distal onychomycosis; not effective when the nail matrix is involved.
  • Limited data suggest the efficacy of once-weekly and twice-weekly application are similar.
  • Usually 6 months for fingernails and 12 months or more for toenails to regrow.
  • Before first application, thoroughly file down, then clean and degrease the affected areas of nail using the cleaning pad provided. Apply the lacquer to the entire surface of the affected nails and allow to dry.
  • Before repeat application, file affected nails as required and clean to remove any remaining lacquer.
  • If working with organic solvents, wear impermeable gloves to protect the lacquer or reapply afterwards.
  • Do not use cosmetic lacquers, artificial nails or occlusive dressings during treatment.

MIMS, 2021

  • The target site of amorphous aescin is the vascular wall. In pathologically raised permeability, amorphous aescin inhibits exudation by reducing the extravasation of fluid into the tissue and accelerating the subsidence of oedema. The mode of action is based on changes in the permeability of the affected capillary walls. In addition, amorphous aescin raises capillary resistance, inhibits inflammatory processes and improves microcirculation.
  • Reduction of localized swelling following injuries.
    • Adults and adolescents >14 years, initially 2 tablets TDS. In milder cases or as maintenance dose, 1 tablet TDS.
    • Children 7-14 years, 1 tablet BD-TDS.
    • Treatment should be continued for 2-3 months for adult and children..
  • Should be taken with food.

The Review of Natural Products, 2021

  • Oral horse chestnut seed extract is effective in the short-term treatment of mild to moderate long-term venous insufficiency, but not for post-thrombotic syndrome. Other investigations focus on the role of the major component aescin in male fertility, antiobesity, and anti-inflammatory effects. Aescin gel has been evaluated for use in bruising.
  • Aescin 20 to 120 mg taken orally has been used for venous insufficiency and is available in tablet form. Oral tinctures and topical gels containing aescin 2% are also available.

    • Birth (at term) - 3 months and >4 kg, IV infusion 25 mg/kg every 8 hours.
    • 3 months and <40 kg, IV 25 mg/kg (maximum 1 g every 8 hours; increase to every 6 hours in severe infections.
    • >40 kg, IV 1 g every 8 hours; increase to every 6 hours in severe infections. Up to 2 g every 6-8 hours can be used.

The Top 100 Drugs, 2015

  • Patients who are allergic to one penicillin will be allergic to all because the hypersensitivity is related to the basic penicillin structure.

British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Clavulanic acid itself has no significant antibacterial activity but, by inactivating beta-lactamases, it makes the combination active against beta-lactamase-producing bacteria that are resistant to amoxicillin. These include resistant strains of Staph. aureus, E. coli, and H. influenzae, as well as many Bacteroides and Klebsiella spp.
  • Avoid in preterm prelabour rupture of the membranes (PROM) - possible increased risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in the neonate.

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Amoxicillin is a derivative of ampicillin and has a similar antibacterial spectrum. It is better absorbed than ampicillin when given by mouth, producing higher plasma and tissue concentrations; unlike ampicillin, absorption is not affected by the presence of food in the stomach.

  • Patients who are allergic to one penicillin will be allergic to all because the hypersensitivity is related to the basic penicillin structure.

Frank Shann Drug Doses, 2017

  • 25 mg/kg (adult, 0.25-1 g) 8 H or 25-40 mg/kg 12 H.

Sarawak Handbook of Medical Emergencies, 2019

  • Antibiotic prophylaxis of endocarditis is indicated for all dental procedures in high-risk patients (e.g. prosthetic cardiac valve, previous infective endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, cardiac transplantation recipients who develop cardiac valvulopathy) that involve manipulation of gingival tissue or the periapical region of teeth or perforation of the oral mucosa.
  • The following dental procedures do not need prophylaxis: routine anesthetic injections through non-infected tissue, taking dental radiographs, placement of removable prosthodontic or orthodontic appliances, adjustment of orthodontic appliances, placement of orthodontic brackets, shedding of deciduous teeth, and bleeding from trauma to the lips or oral mucosa.

    • Allergic to penicillins or ampicillin and unable to take oral medication, cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g IM or IV; OR clindamycin 600 mg IM or IV

drugs.notes:
Product leaflet, accessed 2025 - Ampholip

  • Ampholip is indicated for the treatment of severe systemic and/or deep mycoses in cases where toxicity or renal failure precludes the use of conventional Amphotericin B in effective doses, and in cases where prior systemic antifungal therapy has failed. Fungal infections successfully treated with Ampholip include disseminated candidiasis and aspergillosis.
    • The recommended daily dosage for adults and children is 5 mg/kg given as a single infusion.
    • Ampholip should be administered by intravenous infusion at a rate of 2.5 mg/kg/h. If the infusion time exceeds 2 hours, mix the contents by shaking the infusion bag every 2 hours.
    • Do not use an in-line filter.
  • Ampholip should be stored under refrigeration at 2°C to 8°C. Do not freeze. Protect from direct exposure to light.

Lexidrug, 2025

  • Usual dosage range
    • Adult, IV: 3 to 6 mg/kg once daily.
  • For patients who experience immediate nonanaphylactic infusion-related reactions, premedicate with the following drugs 30 to 60 minutes prior to drug administration: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent ± diphenhydramine; or acetaminophen with diphenhydramine; or hydrocortisone. If the patient experiences rigors during the infusion, meperidine may be administered. Preinfusion administration of 500 ml to 1 L of NS may reduce the risk of nephrotoxicity during amphotericin treatment.
  • AmBisome: Store intact vials ≤25°

British National Formulary 90, 2025

  • The MHRA reminds healthcare professionals that liposomal, pegylated-liposomal, lipid complex, and conventional formulations containing the same drug substance are not interchangeable.
  • Infuse over 30-60 minutes; for doses greater than 5 mg/kg, or to prevent infusion-related reactions - infuse over 2 hours. An in-line filter (pore size no less than 1 micron) may be used.
  • Infusion-related reactions can be managed by stopping the infusion and restarting at a slower rate (over at least 2 hours) or by administering antipyretics, antihistamines or hydrocortisone as premedication.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome®) is less nephrotoxic than conventional amphotericin B.

British National Formulary 90, 2025

  • The MHRA reminds healthcare professionals that liposomal, pegylated-liposomal, lipid complex, and conventional formulations containing the same drug substance are not interchangeable.

  • Acinetobacter baumannii infection, multidrug resistant.
    • Adult, IV: 9 g every 8 hours every 4 hours or 27 g/day over 24 hours as a continuous infusion; alternatively, may consider 3 g every 4 hours, especially if intolerance or toxicity precludes the use of higher doses. Use as part of an appropriate combination regimen whenever possible.

  • Acinetobacter
    • Normal dose, 3 g q6h (infuse over 30-60 minutes).
    • CrCl 31-50 ml/min, unchanged.
    • CrCl 10-30 ml/min, 3 g q12h.

    • HD, 3 g q24h.
    • CVVH, 3 g q12h.
    • CVVHD/CVVHDF, 3 g q6-8h.
  • Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter
    • Normal dose, 9 g q8h (infuse over 4 hours).
    • CrCl 31-50 ml/min, 6 g q8h.
    • CrCl 10-30 ml/min, 6 g q12h.
    • CrCl <10 ml/min, 6 g q12h.
    • HD, 6 g q12h.
    • CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF, 9 g q8h.

Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion, 2021

  • Bacterial infections
    • Length of course depends on the infection and its response to treatment.
    • Birth (at term)-1 week, IV 25-50 mg/kg every 12 hours. For meningitis, use 50-100 mg/kg every 8-12 hours.
    • 1 week-1 month, IV 25-50 mg/kg every 6-8 hours. For meningitis, use 50-100 mg/kg every 6-8 hours.
    • 1 month-18 years, IV/IM 25-50 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) every 6 hours. Use 50 mg/kg every 4-6 hours (maximum 12 g daily) in severe infections.
  • Endocarditis prophylaxis (high-risk)
    • 1 month-18 years, IV/IM 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) as a single dose 30-60 minutes before procedure.

British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Susceptible infections (including bronchitis, urinary-tract infections, otitis media, sinusitis, uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia, salmonellosis)

  • Endocarditis (in combination with another antibiotic if necessary); Listerial meningitis (in combination with another antibiotic)
    • Adult, by intravenous infusion, 2 g every 4 hours.
  • Ampicillin can be given by mouth but less than half the dose is absorbed, and absorption is further decreased by the presence of food in the gut.

drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Essential thrombocythemia
    • Adult, initially 0.5 mg twice daily. Adjust daily dose by 0.5 mg each week to the lowest dose required to achieve a platelet count <600 x 109/L (ideally <400 x 109/L). Maximum 2.5 mg/dose or 10 mg daily.
    • Moderate hepatic impairment, initially, 0.5 mg daily.
  • This drug may cause dizziness. If affected do not drive or operate machinery.
  • Monitor complete blood count and liver and renal function.
  • Assess cardiovascular status before starting anagrelide and monitor for cardiovascular effects during treatment.
  • Platelet count usually begins to fall within 7-14 days of starting treatment; pheresis may be more appropriate when an immediate reduction in platelet count is required.
  • Platelet count increases within 4 days of stopping treatment.

British National Formulary 85, 2023

  • There is an increased risk of potentially fatal thrombosis, including cerebral infarction, due to the rebound in platelet count when anagrelide treatment is discontinued abruptly. The platelet count will typically start to increase within 4 days after discontinuation and return to baseline levels within 1 to 2 weeks, but may rebound above these values.

drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Breast cancer [chemoprevention in postmenopausal women at moderate to high risk] (initiated under specialist supervision)
    • Adult, 1 mg daily for 5 years.
  • Asthenia and drowsiness may affect ability to drive or operate machinery.
  • Assess bone mineral density before treatment and at regular intervals.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Compared with tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors are associated with less endometrial hyperplasia and VTE but more arthralgia, myalgia, bone fractures and cardiovascular disease.
  • Anastrozole and letrozole are selective nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitors; exemestane is an irreversible steroidal aromatase inhibitor. They all decrease tissue estrogen levels by 97-99% with little or no effect on adrenal corticosteroid synthesis, aldosterone or thyroid hormone production at normal doses.
  • Although direct comparisons of efficacy and safety between aromatase inhibitors are limited, major clinical differences appear to be unlikely.

drugs.notes:
Frank Shann Drug Doses, 2017

  • 2-4 mg/kg (adult, 100-200 mg) IV day 1, then 1-2 mg/kg (adult, 50-100 mg) daily.

Lexidrug, 2026

  • Aspergillosis, invasive (salvage therapy)
    • Very limited data available: Infants, children and adolescents, IV: Initial: 1.5 to 3 mg/kg/dose once on day 1; maximum initial dose: 200 mg/dose; on day 2 begin 0.75 to 1.5 mg/kg/dose once daily; maximum dose: 100 mg/dose. Duration of therapy should be individualized based on patient-specific factors including site of infection, immunosuppression, and response to therapy; minimum duration is 6 to 12 weeks.
  • Candidemia; intra-abdominal or peritoneal candidiasis
    • Infants, children and adolescents, IV: Initial: 3 mg/kg/dose once on day 1; maximum initial dose: 200 mg/dose; on day 2 begin 1.5 mg/kg/dose once daily; maximum dose: 100 mg/dose. Duration of therapy should be individualized (based on deep-tissue foci, clinical response, etc.); candidemia should be treated for a minimum of 14 days from the first negative blood culture and resolution of symptoms.

British National Formulary 92, 2026

  • The echinocandin antifungals include anidulafungin, caspofungin and micafungin. They are only active against Aspergillus spp. and Candida spp.; however, anidulafungin and micafungin are not used for the treatment of aspergillosis. Echinocandins are not effective against fungal infections of the CNS.

Sanford Guide, 2021

  • Like other echinocandins, remarkably non-toxic.
  • Most common side-effects: nausea, vomiting, decreased Mg, decreased K and headache in 11-13% of patients.
  • Infusion-related adverse effects, possibly histamine-related (e.g. rash, urticaria, flushing, pruritus, bronchospasm, dyspnea, hypotension). Do not exceed infusion rate of 1.1 mg/min.
  • Risk of metabolic crisis in patients with hereditary fructose intolerance.

MIMS, 2022

  • Store medicinal product in a refrigerator (2°C-8°C). Excursions for up to 96 hours at temperatures up to 25°C are permitted, and the powder can be returned to refrigerated storage.
  • Reconstituted Solution: Chemical and physical in-use stability of the reconstituted solution has been demonstrated for 24 hours at 25°C.
  • From a microbiological point of view, following good aseptic practices, the reconstituted solution can be utilized for up to 24 hours when stored at 25°C.
  • Infusion Solution: Do not freeze.
    • Chemical and physical in-use stability of the infusion solution has been demonstrated for 48 hours at 25°C.
    • From a microbiological point of view, following good aseptic practices, the infusion solution can be utilized for up to 48 hours from preparation when stored at 25°C.

drugs.brandName: Eliquis, Apexib, Apicog, ApiGlo, Apixoke, Apixtra, Checklot, Genexiban, Hemapix, Nexaq, Varexa, Xagulant, Xavi
drugs.indications:
i) Prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in adult patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF), with one or more risk factors, such as prior stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA); age ≥ 75 years; hypertension; diabetes mellitus; symptomatic heart failure (NYHA Class ≥ II)
ii) Treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), and prevention of recurrent DVT and PE in adults for haemodynamically unstable PE patients.
drugs.dosages:
i) 5 mg taken orally twice daily. Dose reduction: 2.5 mg taken orally twice daily in NVAF patients with at least two of the following characteristics: age ≥80 years old, body weight ≤60 kg, or serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL (133 micromole/L)
ii) For treatment of acute DVT and PE: 10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days (max. 20 mg daily) followed by 5 mg twice daily (max. 10 mg daily); For prevention of recurrent DVT and PE: 2.5 mg twice daily (max. 5 mg daily) following completion of 6 months of treatment with apixaban 5 mg twice daily or with another anticoagulant.
drugs.adverseReactions: Eye hemorrhage (including conjunctiva hemorrhage), hemorrhage, hematoma, epistaxis, nausea, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, rectal hemorrhage and gingival bleeding, hematuria, confusion. NPRA Safety Alert (7 Oct 2021): Risk of abnormal uterine bleeding.
drugs.contraindications:
- Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients.
- Active clinically significant active bleeding.
- Hepatic disease associated with coagulopathy and clinically relevant bleeding risk
- Lesion or condition at significant risk of major bleeding such as current or recent gastrointestinal ulceration, presence of malignant neoplasms at high risk of bleeding, recent brain or spinal injury, recent brain, spinal or ophthalmic surgery, recent intracranial hemorrhage, known or suspected esophageal varices, arteriovenous malformations, vascular aneurysms or major intraspinal or intracerebral vascular abnormalities.
- Concomitant treatment with any other anticoagulant agent e.g. unfractionated heparin (UHF), low molecular weight heparins (enoxaparin, dalteparin, etc.), heparin derivatives (fondaparinux, etc.), oral anticoagulants (warfarin, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, etc.) except under the circumstances of switching anticoagulant therapy or when UHF is given at doses necessary to maintain a patent central venous or arterial catheter.
drugs.interactions:
- Inhibitors of CYP3A4 and P-gp such as azoleantimycotics (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole and posaconazole) and HIV protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir).
- Inducers of CYP3A4 and P-gp (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital or St. John's Wort).
- Anticoagulants, platelet aggregation inhibitors and NSAIDs.
- Activated charcoal.
drugs.precautions:
- Hemorrhage risk.
- Interaction with other medicinal products affecting hemostasis.
- Use of thromboprophylactic agents for the treatment of acute ischemic stroke.
- Patients with prosthetic heart valves.
- Surgery and invasive procedures.
- Temporary discontinuation.
- Spinal/epidural anesthesia or puncture.
- Renal impairment.
- Body weight.
- Elderly patients.
- Renal impairment.
- Hepatic impairment.
- Interaction with inhibitors of both CYP3A4 and P-gp.
- Interaction with inducers of both CYP3A4 and P-gp.
- Hip fracture surgery.
- Laboratory parameters (Changes observed in clotting test at the expected therapeutic dose are small and subject to a high degree of variability).
- Information about excipients (apixaban contains lactose. Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose).

NPRA Safety Alert (22 Aug 2025): Risk of Atraumatic Splenic Rupture.
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Patients should be monitored for signs of bleeding or anemia; treatment should be stopped if severe bleeding occurs.
  • The apixaban reversal agent andexanet alfa (Ondexxya®) is available if required; its reversal effects should be monitored using clinical parameters, as anti-FXa assay results may not be reliable.
  • No routine anticoagulant monitoring required (INR tests are unreliable).
  • A clinical trial has shown an increased risk of recurrent thrombotic events associated with rivaroxaban compared with warfarin, in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and a history of thrombosis. There may be a similar risk associated with other DOACs.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Factor Xa inhibitors:
    • Fondaparinux is given by SC injection; apixaban and rivaroxaban are taken orally.
    • Apixaban and rivaroxaban have a similar onset of action and a half-life of approximately 12 hours; however, apixaban is taken twice daily while rivaroxaban is usually taken once daily (twice a day for the first 3 weeks of DVT treatment).
  • You can crush the tablets and mix them in water, apple juice or apple sauce; take them within 4 hours.

Sarawak Handbook of Medical Emergencies, 2019

  • Patient with large anterior MI should be considered for treatment with warfarin/DOACs for 3-6 months.
  • Patients with severe LV dysfunction, AF or left ventricular aneurysm should be treated with warfarin/DOACs long-term to decrease the risk of systemic embolization.
  • Anticoagulation with warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) reduce risk of systemic embolization by almost 70% and should be considered for most AF patients.
  • The evidence does not support the use of antiplatelet agents for the prevention of thromboembolic events in AF. They are mainly used in patients who cannot take anticoagulation therapy for reasons other than bleeding risk.

drugs.indications:
i) Treatment of adult patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis who are candidates for phototherapy or systemic therapy.
ii) Alone or in combination with Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs), for the treatment of active psoriatic arthritis (PsA) in adult patients who have had an inadequate response or who have been intolerant to a prior DMARD therapy.
drugs.prescribingRestrictions:
Indication i) As a second line treatment option in patients who have contraindications/treatment goals not achieved/adverse events to methotrexate.
Indication ii) To be prescribed by Rheumatologists only
drugs.dosages: 30 mg twice daily taken orally approximately 12 hours apart. Refer to the latest product insert for initial dose titration.
drugs.adverseReactions: Diarrhoea and nausea, upper respiratory tract infections, headache, and tension headache, psychiatric disorder, body weight loss.
drugs.contraindications: In patients with known hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients; during pregnancy and in nursing women.
drugs.interactions: Apremilast exposure is decreased when administered concomitantly with strong inducers of CYP3A4 (e.g. rifampicin, phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, phenytoin and St. John's Wort) and may result in reduced clinical response.
drugs.precautions: Paediatric use, use in the elderly, weight decrease, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, depression, renal function and use in patients with lactose intolerance.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis; Active psoriatic arthritis with inadequate response to other antirheumatics (may be used with methotrexate)
    • Adults, initially 10 mg once on day 1, then 10 mg twice on day 2, then increase by 10 mg each day to 30 mg twice a day.
    • CrCl <30 ml/minute, initially 10 mg once a day for 3 days, then 20 mg once a day for 2 days, then 30 mg once a day
    • Consider stopping treatment if there is no response after 24 weeks.
  • Increase dosage slowly to limit GI adverse effects (e.g. diarrhea).
    • Diarrhea affects around 15% of patients and is usually mild-to-moderate. Most cases occurred in the first 2 weeks and resolved within 4 weeks but some were prolonged for months.
  • Monitor weight regularly; consider stopping treatment if significant weight loss occurs in psoriasis, benefit may be seen within 2 weeks and maximum response by 24-28 weeks; response may start to decrease after 32 weeks.
  • In psoriatic arthritis, benefit may be seen within 4 weeks (based on limited data) and response appears to be maintained (in studies of up to 1 year).

British National Formulary 84, 2022

  • Swallow this medicine whole. Do not chew or crush.
  • A review of evidence from clinical trials and postmarketing cases has suggested a causal association between apremilast and suicidal thoughts and behaviour.

    • CrCl <30 ml/minute, initially 10 mg once a day for 3 days, then 20 mg once a day for 2 days, then 30 mg once a day

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Emollients soothe, smooth and hydrate the skin and are indicated for all dry or scaling disorders. Their effects are short lived and they should be applied frequently even after improvement occurs. They are useful in dry and eczematous disorders, and to a lesser extent in psoriasis.
  • Preparations such as aqueous cream and emulsifying ointment can be used as soap substitutes for hand washing and in the bath; the preparation is rubbed on the skin before rinsing off completely,
  • The addition of a bath oil may also be helpful.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Ideally, moisturisers should be cosmetically acceptable, free from common contact allergens and easy to apply.
  • Moisturisers come in various forms, including ointments, creams, lotions and bath oils. In general, the heavier or greasier the preparation, the more effective it is.
  • Unlike most ointments, creams and lotions contain preservative that may rarely cause contact allergic dermatitis.
  • Ensure patients do not use moisturisers containing sodium lauryl sulfate (e.g. aqueous cream, emulsifying ointment) as it can damage the skin barrier and cause irritation.
  • Cetomacrogol aqueous cream is also known as sorbolene cream.

drugs.brandName: Abilify, Abilimac, Apalife, Arian, Aricog, Arilift, AripMT, Ariptor, Arisa (Orodispersible Tablet)
drugs.indications:
i) Treatment of acute episodes of schizophrenia and for maintenance of clinical improvement during continuation therapy.
ii) Treatment of acute manic episodes associated with bipolar I disorder
drugs.dosages:
Schizophrenia, 10 or 15 mg/day. Maintenance dose: 15 mg/day.
Bipolar mania, starting dose: 15 or 30 mg/day. Dose adjustment should occur at intervals of not less than 24 hour
drugs.adverseReactions: Insomnia, restlessness, headache, dizziness, akathisia, somnolence, sedation, tremor, extrapyramidal disorder, blurred vision, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, vomiting, constipation, dyspepsia, asthenia/fatigue, weight gain, anxiety diabetic ketoacidosis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, seizure, peripheral edema
drugs.contraindications: Patients who are hypersensitive to aripiprazole or to any of the excipients.
drugs.interactions: Enhance effect of antihypertensive agents, alcohol, quinidine, ketoconazole, carbamazepine
drugs.precautions: Suicide, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, seizure disorder, diabetes mellitus, CV disease, cerebrovascular disease, dementia-related psychosis and CV adverse events in elderly. May disrupt body's ability to increase/reduce core body temperature. Dysphagia, pregnancy & lactation. May impair ability to drive or operate machinery. Safety and efficacy have not been established in children less than 13 years of age
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Schizophrenia
    • Adult, 10-15 mg once daily; usual dose 15 mg once daily (max. per dose 30 mg once daily).
  • Treatment and recurrence prevention of mania
    • Adult, 15 mg once daily, increased if necessary up to 30 mg once daily.
  • Dose adjustments due to interactions
    • Manufacturers advises double the dose with concurrent use of potent inducers of CYP3A4.
    • Manufacturer advises reduce dose by half with concurrent use of potent inhibitors of CYP3A4 or CYP2D6.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2021

  • Aripiprazole is a partial agonist at D2 with high affinity for the D3 As a result, it is not associated with hyperprolactinemia.
  • Aripiprazole has a low risk of most forms of EPS, including tardive dyskinesia. Is associated with a high incidence of akathisia.
  • Aripiprazole has been associated with pathological gambling and other compulsive behaviors, which may be related to its affinity for D3.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Taking your antipsychotic medicine regularly is important:
    • because stopping or taking it irregularly is associated with high risk of relapse and suicide.
    • in order to prevent an episode, rather than taking it after symptoms occur.
  • This medicine may cause drowsiness and may increase the effects of alcohol, cannabis or sleeping tablets. Do not drive or operate machinery if you are affected.
  • You may feel dizzy on standing when taking this medicine. Get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimize this; sit or lie down if you become dizzy.
  • Antipsychotics may increase the QT interval, increasing the risk of arrhythmia and sudden death, particularly when given IV: aripiprazole, brexpiprazole and lurasidone have little or no effect while amisulpride, droperidol, haloperidol and ziprasidone are the most likely to prolong the QT interval.

drugs.indications: Relapsed acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML).
drugs.prescribingRestrictions: To be prescribed by consultant hematologist only.
drugs.dosages: Induction: 0.15 mg/kg/day IV until bone marrow remission. Total induction dose ≤60 doses. Consolidation: 0.15 mg/kg/day IV for 25 doses in 5 weeks (5 days per week, followed by 2 days interruption; treatment should begin 3-6 weeks after completion of induction therapy).
drugs.adverseReactions: Leukocytosis, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain), fatigue, edema, hyperglycemia, dyspnea, cough, rash or itching, headaches, and dizziness, complete atrioventricular block, prolonged QT interval, Torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmia, anemia grade 3 & 4, disseminated intravascular coagulation grade 3 & 4, febrile neutropenia, neutropenia, grade 3 & 4, thrombocytopenia, grade 3 & 4, hepatotoxicity, immune hypersensitivity reaction, renal failure, renal impairment, pleural effusion, retinoic acid - acute promyelocytic leukemia syndrome
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to arsenic.
drugs.interactions: Caution if co-administered with medications that prolong QT interval or lead to electrolyte abnormalities
drugs.precautions:
Hepatic impairment. Severe renal impairment (CrCl less than 30 ml/min), higher exposure, dose reduction may be necessary. APL differentiation syndrome. ECG abnormalities, electrolyte imbalance, hyperleukocytosis, AV block. Pregnancy and lactation.

Monitoring requirement:
i) FBC daily for first 2 weeks then on alternate days during induction and weekly during consolidation
ii) Coagulation profile on alternate days for the first 2 weeks then weekly during induction phase
iii) Liver function test, electrolytes twice a week during induction then weekly during consolidation
iv) ECG pre-treatment and when clinically indicated.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Arsenic trioxide prolongs the QT interval and increases the risk of arrhythmia; correct risk factors for prolonged QT interval before and during treatment if possible and use with caution.
  • Watch for signs and symptoms of peripheral neuropathy

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Signs and symptoms of differentiation syndrome (leucocyte activation syndrome) include unexplained fever, dyspnea, weight gain, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural or pericardial effusions, with or without leukocytosis. Treat with high dose corticosteroids.
  • Manufacturer advises effective contraception during treatment in men and women.

Infant and child weighing 5 kg to less than 35 kg, A 6 dose regimen with 1 to 3 tablets per dose, depending on bodyweight.

drugs.notes:

  • First line for uncomplicated malaria.

drugs.indications: Treatment of acute uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, resulting either from P. falciparum mono-infection or mixed infection with P. vivax.
drugs.dosages:
Weight 5-8 kg, Age 6-11 months, Dose: One tablet 25/55 mg OD x 3 days
Weight: 9-17 kg, Age 1-6 years, Dose: Two tablet 25/55 mg OD x 3 days
Weight:18-29 kg, Age 7-12 years, Dose: One tablet 100/220 mg OD x 3 days
Weight ≥30 kg, Age ≥13 years, Dose: Two tablet 100/220 mg OD x 3 days

drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients. Known hypersensitivity to quinine, quinidine or any artemisinin. Concurrent or recent ketoconazole therapy, due to the increased risk of prolongation of the QTc interval

drugs.precautions: Patients with underlying cardiac conduction defects or known cardiac arrhythmias. drugs.indications: Treatment of severe malaria in adults and children.
drugs.dosages: 2.4 mg of artesunate/kg body weight, by intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM) injection, at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily until oral treatment can be substituted. For adults and children with severe malaria or who are unable to tolerate oral medicines, artesunate 2.4 mg/kg body weight IV or IM given on admission (time = 0), then at 12 hrs and 24 hrs, then once a day for 5-7 days is the recommended treatment.
drugs.adverseReactions: Transient and reversible reticulocytopenia, drug fever, rash, bradycardia, transient 1st-degree heart block and reversible elevation of serum transaminases.

drugs.indications: Asciminib is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukaemia in chronic phase (Ph+ CML-CP) previously treated with two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
drugs.prescribingRestrictions:
i. As a third line treatment for adult Ph+ CML-CP patients with pre-existing CV risks and/or CV events.
ii. To be prescribed by Haematologist only.
drugs.dosages: 40 mg twice daily at approximately 12‐hour intervals.
drugs.adverseReactions: Musculoskeletal pain, upper respiratory tract infections, thrombocytopaenia, fatigue, headache, arthralgia, rash, increased pancreatic enzymes, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, neutropenia, hypertension, anaemia, cardiac failure congestive, lower respiratory tract infections, pyrexia, pancreatitis, mesenteric artery thrombosis and ischemic stroke.
drugs.contraindications: None.
drugs.interactions: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole), CYP3A4 substrates (midazolam), CYP2C9 substrates (warfarin), substrates of OATP1B or BCRP (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin).
drugs.precautions: Myelosuppression, pancreatic toxicity, cardiovascular toxicity, hypertension, hypersensitivity, embryo-fetal toxicity.
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 85, 2023

  • Chronic phase Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia (initiated by a specialist)
    • Adult, 80 mg once daily, to be taken at approximately the same time each day or alternatively 40 mg twice daily, to be taken at approximately 12-hour intervals. For dose adjustments, treatment interruption or discontinuation due to side-effects, consult product literature.
  • Scemblix tablets should be taken without food. Patients should avoid eating for at least 2 hours before and 1 hour after taking a dose.
  • If a once-daily dose is more than 12 hours late, or a twice-daily dose is more than 6 hours late, the missed dose should not be taken and the next dose should be taken at the normal time.
  • Females of childbearing potential should use effective contraception during and for at least 3 days after last treatment.
  • An EU wide review has concluded that BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors can cause hepatitis B reactivation.

Lexicomp, 2024

  • The AUC and Cmax of asciminib decreased by 62% and 68%, respectively, with a high-fat meal (1000 calories, 50% fat) and by 30% and 35%, respectively, with a low-fat meal (400 calories, 25% fat) compared to the fasted state. Management: Administer on an empty stomach.

drugs.indications: Vitamin C deficiency
drugs.dosages: Adult, 100-250 mg once or twice daily. Child, 100 mg three times daily for one week followed by 100 mg daily until symptoms abate.
drugs.adverseReactions: In large doses, gastrointestinal disturbances, renal calcium oxalate calculi formation
drugs.contraindications: History of hyperoxaluria
drugs.interactions: Antacids, aspirin, contraceptives combination, cyanocobalamin, deferoxamine, gentamicin, haloperidol, iron, levodopa, methotrexate, warfarin
drugs.precautions: Use cautiously in patients with pre-existing kidney stone disease, erythrocyte G6PD deficiency, haemochromatosis, thalassemia or sideroblastic anemia and avoid rapid intravenous injections
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2024

  • Burns, nutritional supplement (off-label use)
    • Adult, 500 mg twice daily; continue until burn wounds are healed or patient is discharged.
  • Nutritional supplement
    • Adult, 100 to 1500 mg daily; dosage may vary depending on dosage form; consult specific product labeling.
  • Scurvy
    • Adult, 100 to 300 mg daily until body stores are replenished; dose and duration of therapy should be individualized; doses as low as 10 mg may be effective.
  • Administer with food.

British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Prevention of scurvy
    • Adult, 25-75 mg daily.
  • Treatment of scurvy
    • Adult, not less than 250 mg daily in divided doses.
  • It is rarely necessary to prescribe more than 100 mg daily except early in the treatment of scurvy.

Micromedex, 2024

  • Burn (severe)
    • Adult, 200 to 500 mg/day up to 1 to 2 g/day IM/IV/SC or orally until healing or completion of grafting.
  • Iron supplement therapy; adjunct
    • Adult, 500 mg orally once daily is the labeled dosage; ascorbic acid can enhance oral iron absorption when taken concomitantly with oral iron (guideline dosage).

The Top 100 Drugs, 2015

  • Iron is best absorbed in its ferrous state (Fe2+) in the duodenum and jejunum. Its absorption is increased by stomach acid and dietary acids such as ascorbic acid (vitamin C).

drugs.indications:
For second or third line treatment in adult for:
i) Schizophrenia
ii) Bipolar Disorder - Monotherapy: Acute treatment of manic or mixed episodes associated with Bipolar I disorder. - Adjunctive therapy: As adjunctive therapy with either lithium or valproate for the acute treatment of manic or mixed episodes associated with Bipolar I Disorder.
drugs.dosages:
i) Schizophrenia: - Acute treatment in adults: Recommended starting and target dose of asenapine is 5 mg given twice daily. - Maintenance dose: 5 mg twice daily.
ii) Bipolar Disorder: - Monotherapy: 10 mg twice daily. Adjunctive therapy: 5 mg twice daily with lithium or valproate. Dose can be increased to 10 mg twice daily based on clinical response.
drugs.adverseReactions: Akathisia, oral hypoesthesia, somnolence, dizziness, extrapyramidal symptoms other than akathisia, weight gain, dysgeusia, oral hypoesthesia, dystonia.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to asenapine.
drugs.interactions: Other centrally-acting drugs. May enhance the effect of certain antihypertensive agents. Fluvoxamine. Co-administration with CYP2D6 substrates & inhibitors. Alcohol.
drugs.precautions: Cerebrovascular adverse events, dementia-related psychosis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, hyperglycemia & diabetes mellitus. Monitor weight regularly. Hypersensitivity reaction such as anaphylaxis, angioedema, hypotension, tachycardia, swollen tongue, dyspnea, wheezing and rash. Orthostatic hypotension, syncope & other hemodynamic effects. Leukopenia, neutropenia & agranulocytosis. History of cardiac arrhythmias. Hyperprolactinemia, seizures. Conditions that may contribute to an elevation in core body temp. Suicide, dysphagia. Hepatic impairment. May impair ability to drive or operate machinery. Pregnancy & lactation. Children <18 yr, elderly.
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2021

  • Sublingual tablets should be placed under the tongue and allowed to completely dissolve. Do not split, crush, chew, or swallow. Avoid eating or drinking for at least 10 minutes after administration.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Absorption of asenapine is very low if the wafer is swallowed instead of being taken sublingually
  • The inside of your mouth may feel tingly or numb for about an hour after taking the wafer.
  • Taking your antipsychotic medicine regularly is important:
    • because stopping or taking it irregularly is associated with high risk of relapse and suicide.
    • in order to prevent an episode, rather than taking it after symptoms occur.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics 2021

  • Asenapine has been associated with a high risk of orthostasis and sedation.
  • There has also been a warning about the risk of hypersensitivity reactions with asenapine.
  • Asenapine use is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.

ii) Bipolar Disorder: - Monotherapy: 10 mg twice daily. Adjunctive therapy: 5 mg twice daily with lithium or valproate. Dose can be increased to 10 mg twice daily based on clinical response.
drugs.adverseReactions: Akathisia, oral hypoesthesia, somnolence, dizziness, extrapyramidal symptoms other than akathisia, weight gain, dysgeusia, oral hypoesthesia, dystonia.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to asenapine.
drugs.interactions: Other centrally-acting drugs. May enhance the effect of certain antihypertensive agents. Fluvoxamine. Co-administration with CYP2D6 substrates & inhibitors. Alcohol.
drugs.precautions: Cerebrovascular adverse events, dementia-related psychosis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, hyperglycemia & diabetes mellitus. Monitor weight regularly. Hypersensitivity reaction such as anaphylaxis, angioedema, hypotension, tachycardia, swollen tongue, dyspnea, wheezing and rash. Orthostatic hypotension, syncope & other hemodynamic effects. Leukopenia, neutropenia & agranulocytosis. History of cardiac arrhythmias. Hyperprolactinemia, seizures. Conditions that may contribute to an elevation in core body temp. Suicide, dysphagia. Hepatic impairment. May impair ability to drive or operate machinery. Pregnancy & lactation. Children <18 yr, elderly.
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2021

  • Sublingual tablets should be placed under the tongue and allowed to completely dissolve. Do not split, crush, chew, or swallow. Avoid eating or drinking for at least 10 minutes after administration.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Absorption of asenapine is very low if the wafer is swallowed instead of being taken sublingually
  • The inside of your mouth may feel tingly or numb for about an hour after taking the wafer.
  • Taking your antipsychotic medicine regularly is important:
    • because stopping or taking it irregularly is associated with high risk of relapse and suicide.
    • in order to prevent an episode, rather than taking it after symptoms occur.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics 2021

  • Asenapine has been associated with a high risk of orthostasis and sedation.
  • There has also been a warning about the risk of hypersensitivity reactions with asenapine.
  • Asenapine use is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment.

drugs.genericName: Asfotase Alfa 100 mg/ml Solution for Injection
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Pediatric-onset hypophosphatasia (initiated by a specialist)
    • Adult, by subcutaneous injection, 2 mg/kg 3 times a week, alternatively 1 mg/kg 6 times a week, dosing frequency depends on body-weight - consult product literature for further information.
  • Manufacturer advises max. 1 ml per injection site; administer multiple injections if more than 1 ml is required.
  • Hypersensitivity reactions, including signs and symptoms consistent with anaphylaxis, have occurred within minutes of administration and can occur in patients on treatment for more than one year; if these reactions occur, manufacturer advises immediate discontinuation of treatment and initiation of appropriate medical treatment. For information on re-administration, consult product literature.
  • Manufacturer advises store in a refrigerator (2-8°C).

drugs.genericName: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) Root Extract 300 mg Capsule
drugs.notes:
Product website, accessed 2020 - Vitamode

  • Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an Ayurvedic herb and medicinal plant, with a 4,000-year usage history. Also known as Indian ginseng for its adaptive abilities, this herb is mostly harvested for its roots that contain active constituents known as withanolides. The withanolides make ashwagandha an excellent adaptogen that mainly promotes balance in the body addressing stress and fatigue while also improving muscle strength, energy, sexual vitality and cognitive health.
    • Adult, take 1-2 capsules once daily, after food.

The Review of Natural Products, 2020

  • Ashwagandha has been used as an adaptogen, diuretic, and sedative and is available in the United States as a dietary supplement. Trials supporting its clinical use are limited; however, many in vitro and animal experiments suggest effects on the immune, endocrine, and CNS systems, as well as in the pathogenesis of cancer and inflammatory conditions.
    • Dosing information is limited. W. somnifera root powder has generally been used at daily dosages of 120 mg to 2 g in combination with other preparations.
  • Abortifacient properties have been reported for ashwagandha.

drugs.genericName: Aspirin 100 mg and Glycine 45 mg Tablet
drugs.brandName: Cardiprin, Cardin (Orodispersible Tablet), Glyprin (Dispersible), Viquprin, Wincardia (Dispersible)
drugs.indications:
i) Prevention of myocardial infarct, stroke, vascular occlusion and deep vein thrombosis.
ii) Transient ischemic attacks
drugs.dosages: 1 tablet daily
drugs.adverseReactions: Nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, GI ulceration, hematemesis, melaena. Occasionally hepatotoxicity
drugs.contraindications: Bleeding disorders. Hypersensitivity to salicylate
drugs.interactions: Alcohol, dipyridamole, metoclopramide, metoprolol, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, corticosteroids, coumarin anticoagulants, sulphonylureas, methotrexate, phenytoin, valproic acid, probenecid, sulphinpyrazone
drugs.precautions: Dyspepsia, gastric mucosal lesions, hemorrhagic disorders, gout, intolerant to aspirin, renal or hepatic impairment, asthma and G6PD deficiency
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Aspirin reduces the risk of serious vascular events (including stroke, MI and vascular death) by 13% in people with previous TIA or ischaemic stroke; give to all patients unless contraindicated.
  • Weigh risk of cardiovascular events versus bleeding risk; aspirin may be stopped 7 days before surgery to decrease risk of bleeding; however, its withdrawal may increase risk of cardiac events.

Martindale The Complete Drug Reference, 2020

  • Glycine is used as an ingredient of some aspirin preparations with the object of reducing gastric irritation.

British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Owing to an association with Reye's syndrome, manufacturer advises aspirin-containing preparations should not be given to children under 16 years, unless specifically indicated, e.g. for Kawasaki disease.

drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Mild to moderate pain; pyrexia
    • Adult, 300-900 mg every 4-6 hours as required; maximum 4 g per day.
  • Owing to an association with Reye's syndrome, manufacturer advises aspirin-containing preparations should not be given to children under 16 years, unless specifically indicated, e.g. for Kawasaki disease.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Dosage - ACS and history of symptomatic atherosclerosis
    • Adult
      • Acute conditions, initially 150-300 mg once daily may be required (e.g. ACS, acute ischemic stroke, placement of intracoronary stent).
      • Long term, 75-150 mg once daily (low-dose aspirin). When given with ticagrelor, the dose is 75-100 mg once daily,
    • Child, 1-5 mg/kg once daily, not to exceed 150 mg daily.
  • Prevention of pre-eclampsia
    • 75-150 mg once daily (low-dose aspirin), starting at 12-16 weeks gestation and continuing until delivery.
  • Taking with or after food may reduce stomach upset.
  • Remove tablets from packaging just before use as aspirin can break down rapidly if it isn't protected by the packaging.
  • Mix dispersible tablets in water immediately before use.
  • If you develop swollen ankles, difficulty in breathing, black stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, stop taking the medicine and contact your doctor without delay.
  • Aspirin reduces the risk of serious vascular events (including stroke, MI and vascular death) by 13% in people with previous TIA or ischaemic stroke; give to all patients unless contraindicated.
  • Weigh risk of cardiovascular events versus bleeding risk; aspirin may be stopped 7 days before surgery to decrease risk of bleeding; however, its withdrawal may increase risk of cardiac events.
  • There is no evidence that enteric coated products decrease risk of GI bleeding.

Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion, 2021

  • Kawasaki disease
    • 2 g/kg IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) is the main treatment.
    • Aspirin has been used in Kawasaki disease for many years but its dose in the acute phase is still debated: 30-50 mg/kg daily is used in Japan, the UK and other centres, while 80-100 mg/kg daily is used in the US although there is no advantage from using the higher dose.
    • The antiplatelet dose traditionally used is 3-5 mg/kg once daily but doses of 1-2 mg/kg daily have also been used.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2021

  • Prevention: Women at high risk of preeclampsia development may take aspirin 60-80 mg beginning in late first trimester; a study showed lower incidence of preeclampsia development in women who were administered 150 mg of aspirin from 11 to 14 weeks of gestation to 36 weeks.

Lexicomp, 2021

  • Pericarditis, acute or recurrent (treatment) (off-label use): Note: Preferred over other NSAIDs in patients with ischemic heart disease since aspirin is required. If pericarditis occurs after an MI, avoid anti-inflammatory doses for 7 to 10 days. Use acetaminophen for analgesia unless symptoms require acute treatment with an NSAID.
    • Adult, immediate release: Initial: 650 mg to 1 g every 8 hours until resolution of symptoms for at least 24 hours and normalization of inflammatory biomarkers (e.g. C-reactive therapy); initial therapy typically lasts for at least 1 to 2 weeks. Gradually taper off over several weeks by decreasing each dose by 250 to 500 mg every 1 to 2 weeks; during taper, ensure patient remains asymptomatic and inflammatory biomarkers are normal. Use in combination with colchicine. In patients at risk of NSAID-related GI toxicity, prophylaxis (generally with a proton pump inhibitor) is recommended.

drugs.genericName: Astaxanthin 3 mg, Bilberry Extract 25 mg and Vitamin E 10.5 IU Capsule
drugs.notes:
Product website, accessed 2020 - Vitamode

  • Vitamode® Asta-i-Care Capsule is a triple antioxidant combo of astaxanthin, bilberry extract and vitamin E which are beneficial for protecting the eyes from daily fatigue caused by over usage or exposure to free radicals.
    • Adult, take 1-2 capsules once daily, after food.

The Review of Natural Products, 2020

  • Traditional uses of dried bilberry fruit include supportive treatment of short-term, nonspecific diarrhea when administered as a tea, and as a topical decoction for inflammation of the mucous membranes of the mouth and throat. Folkloric use of the berries in cough preparations in the 15th century and use in diabetes at the end of the 19th century has been reported.
  • During World War II, British Royal Air Force pilots ate bilberry preserves before night missions in the belief that bilberry would improve their vision. Some European health care providers later recommended bilberry extracts for other eye complaints.
  • Clinical studies are limited. Interest has focused on antioxidant potential in cancer and cardiovascular conditions, and other applications may exist in diabetes, as well as in inflammatory bowel and ocular conditions.
    • Typical bilberry products are standardized to 25% anthocyanoside content, and 100 g of fresh fruit contains anthocyanin content 300 to 700 mg. Limited clinical studies have evaluated supplemental bilberry 100 to 500 g over 1 to 8 weeks' duration.
  • Long-term use of bilberry leaves is suspected to be hazardous. No cytotoxic effect was seen on corneal epithelial cells exposed to bilberry extract. Low concentrations of bilberry extract were protective in animal models of reperfusion injury; however, high concentrations increased sequelae of the reperfusion injury.

drugs.genericName: Atazanavir 300 mg and Ritonavir 100 mg Film-coated Tablet
drugs.indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infected, antiretroviral treatment experienced adults, in combination with other antiretroviral medicinal products.
drugs.prescribingRestrictions: For Infectious Disease Physicians use, in patients with treatment failure on NNRTI regimen.
drugs.dosages: One tablet (Atazanavir 300 mg and Ritonavir 100 mg) taken orally once daily with food.
drugs.adverseReactions: Commonly reported adverse drug reactions include the gastrointestinal system (diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, and abdominal pain), the nervous system (headache, dizziness, dysgeusia, and peripheral or oral paraesthesia), and general asthenia or fatigue. Other highly prevalent clinical effects include respiratory symptoms (pharyngitis, cough), musculoskeletal pain (arthralgia, back pain, myalgia), and dermatological reactions (pruritus, maculopapular rash). Patients also commonly experience metabolic and haematological shifts, such as hyperlipidaemia, dehydration, and thrombocytopenia, alongside hepatobiliary complications including jaundice, hepatitis, and elevated blood bilirubin.
drugs.contraindications: Atazanavir/ritonavir is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to its active substances or excipients, and in individuals with moderate to severe hepatic insufficiency. Co-administration is contraindicated with St. John’s wort (Hypericum perforatum), hepatitis C therapeutics containing grazoprevir (e.g., elbasvir/grazoprevir) or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, and medications products that are highly dependent on CYP3A for clearance due to the risk of serious or life-threatening adverse events.
drugs.interactions: As a potent CYP3A inhibitor, ritonavir can substantially increase plasma concentrations of concurrently administered CYP3A-metabolized drugs (particularly those with high first-pass metabolism), which can lead to fatal toxicities (e.g., when combined with sedative-hypnotics, antiarrhythmics, or ergot alkaloids). Conversely, co-administration with CYP3A4 inducers or inhibitors may significantly alter atazanavir and ritonavir levels, resulting in either heightened drug toxicity or subtherapeutic exposure, which risks a loss of therapeutic efficacy and the development of viral resistance.
drugs.precautions: Monitor liver function closely, particularly in patients with chronic hepatitis B or C, due to the elevated risk of severe hepatic reactions. Reversible hyperbilirubinemia is common; however, dose reduction is not recommended, and co-administration with indinavir is contraindicated. Cardiac monitoring is advised due to potential PR and QT interval prolongations, especially in patients with pre-existing conduction abnormalities or structural heart disease. Regular renal monitoring is required given the risks of chronic kidney disease and nephrolithiasis; this regimen is not recommended for patients undergoing haemodialysis. Therapy must be discontinued immediately if severe skin reactions (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS) or pancreatitis develop. Additional clinical monitoring is warranted for cholelithiasis, metabolic shifts (blood glucose, lipids, weight), and diarrhoea, which may compromise drug absorption. Clinicians should also assess for Immune Reactivation Syndrome, osteonecrosis, and increased bleeding episodes in haemophiliac patients.

drugs.contraindications:

drugs.indications:
i) Hypertension
ii) Arrhythmias
iii) Angina pectoris
iii) Myocardial infarction
drugs.dosages:
i), ii) & iii) 50-100 mg daily
iv) Dosing is individualized and according to product insert/protocol.
drugs.adverseReactions: Chronic heart failure, AV block, bradycardia, bronchospasm, dizziness, vertigo, nausea, fatigue, diarrhea
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to atenolol products, bradycardia, 2nd and 3rd degree AV block overt cardiac failure, cardiogenic shock, metabolic acidosis, severe peripheral circulatory disturbances, sick sinus syndrome
drugs.interactions: Clonidine, catecholamine-depleting agents, beta-blockers
drugs.precautions: Avoid abrupt withdrawal; gradual withdrawal over a period of 1 to 2 weeks is recommended. Bronchospastic disease, congestive heart failure, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis. Patients receiving clonidine - discontinue atenolol several days prior to withdrawal of clonidine. Peripheral vascular and renal disease
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Use of atenolol for migraine prophylaxis is an unlicensed indication.
    • Adult, 50-200 mg daily in divided doses.
  • Some beta-blockers are lipid soluble and some are water soluble. Water-soluble beta-blockers (such as atenolol, celiprolol hydrochloride, nadolol, and sotalol hydrochloride) are less likely to enter the brain, and may therefore cause less sleep disturbance and nightmares. Water-soluble beta-blockers are excreted by the kidneys and dosage reduction is often necessary in renal impairment.
  • Beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm and should therefore usually be avoided in patients with a history of asthma. When there is no suitable alternative, it may be necessary for a patient with well-controlled asthma, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (without significant reversible airways obstruction), to receive treatment with a beta-blocker for a co-existing condition (e.g. heart failure or following myocardial infarction). In this situation, a cardioselective beta-blocker should be selected and initiated at a low dose by a specialist; the patient should be closely monitored for adverse effects. Atenolol, bisoprolol fumarate, metoprolol tartrate, nebivolol, and (to a lesser extent) acebutolol, have less effect on the beta2 (bronchial) receptors and are, therefore, relatively cardioselective, but they are not cardiospecific. They have a lesser effect on airways resistance but are not free of this side-effect.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine may cause dizziness or tiredness especially at the start of treatment or when the dose is increased; if affected, do not drive or operate machinery.
  • If you feel dizzy, get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimise this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy.
  • Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly unless your doctor tells you to.
  • When stopping treatment, reduce dosage gradually, e.g. over at least 2 weeks; avoid abrupt withdrawal as it may exacerbate angina, or precipitate rebound hypertension, MI or arrhythmias.

drugs.indications: Atezolizumab, in combination with Bevacizumab, is indicated for the treatment of patients with unresectable or metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who have not received prior systemic therapy
drugs.prescribingRestrictions: Only for patients with Child-Pugh A
drugs.dosages: The recommended dose of atezolizumab in combination therapy is 1200 mg administered every 3 weeks, all doses administered as IV infusion.
drugs.adverseReactions: ADRs identified in clinical trials (not reported in monotherapy trials) associated with the use of atezolizumab in combination therapy: Anemia, lymphopenia, neutropenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, constipation, stomatitis, oedema peripheral, lung infection, blood alkaline phosphatase increased, hypomagnesemia, dizziness, dysgeusia, peripheral neuropathy, syncope, proteinuria, dysphonia, nasopharyngitis, alopecia, hypertension
drugs.contraindications: Contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to atezolizumab or any of the excipients
drugs.interactions: No formal pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction studies have been conducted with atezolizumab. Since atezolizumab is cleared from the circulation through catabolism, no metabolic drug-drug interactions are expected
drugs.precautions: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, Immune-mediated pneumonitis, Immune-mediated hepatitis, Immune- mediated colitis, Immune-mediated endocrinopathies, Immune-mediated meningoencephalitis, Immune-mediated neuropathies, Immune-mediated pancreatitis, Immune-mediated myocarditis, Immune-mediated myositis, Immune- mediated nephritis, Infusion related reactions, Immune-mediated severe cutaneous adverse reactions, Immune-mediated pericardial disorders, Special populations (e.g. patients with autoimmune disease), embryofetal toxicity.
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 86, 2023

  • Urothelial carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, small cell lung cancer, breast cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma
    • Adult, by intravenous infusion, specialist drug- access specialist resources for dosing information.
  • Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), including cases of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), have been reported in patients treated with immunostimulant antineoplastic drugs, such as atezolizumab. Healthcare professionals are advised to monitor patients for suspected severe skin reactions and exclude other causes. Patients should be advised to seek urgent medical attention if severe skin reactions occur. If a SCAR is suspected, atezolizumab therapy should be withheld and the patient referred to a specialist for diagnosis and treatment. Atezolizumab should be permanently discontinued for any grade confirmed SJS or TEN, and for any grade 4 SCAR. Caution is recommended when considering the use of atezolizumab in patients with a history of severe or life-threatening SCAR associated with other immunostimulant antineoplastic drugs.
  • Manufacturer advises most immune-related adverse reactions are reversible and managed by temporarily stopping treatment and administration of a corticosteroid.
  • Manufacturer advises effective contraception in women of childbearing potential, during treatment and for 5 months after stopping treatment.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Infusion-related reactions include dyspnea, fever, chills, hypotension, wheezing and flushing. Stop the infusion if symptoms occur and treat symptomatically. If reaction is severe, stop treatment permanently. If reaction is mild-to-moderate, restart atezolizumab at a slower infusion rate with close monitoring; consider premedication with paracetamol and an antihistamine before further doses.

  • Tecentriq should be protected from light.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Generally reserve for ADHD patients who do not respond to, or are intolerant of, psychostimulants.
  • Give as a single dose in the morning or as 2 doses (in the morning and late afternoon).
  • Maximum of 1.4 mg/kg (not to exceed 100 mg) daily. Avoid maximum dose in people with moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment or taking potent CYP2D6 inhibitors like fluoxetine and paroxetine.
  • This medicine may make you feel drowsy or dizzy; do not drive or operate machinery if you are affected.

  • Following reports of suicidal thoughts and behavior, patients and their carers should be informed about the risk and told to report clinical worsening, suicidal thoughts or behavior, irritability, agitation or depression.

Adults and adolescents more than 70 kg, initially 40 mg/day for at least 7 days then increased according to response. Maintenance: 80 mg/day. Max 100 mg/ day.
drugs.adverseReactions: Gastrointestinal disorder or cardiovascular disorders, weight loss, decreased appetite, weight loss. Nervous system disorders such as dizziness, headache, insomnia, somnolence, mood swings, urinary retention, dysmenorrhea, ejaculation disorder. Orthostatic hypotension and syncope, psychiatric disorders such as irritability, suicidal thought
drugs.contraindications: Concomitant use with MAOIs. Narrow-angle glaucoma, liver injury, jaundice
drugs.interactions: MAOIs, CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine), salbutamol, pressor agents, drugs that affect noradrenaline, methylphenidate, drugs that affect gastric pH, drugs highly bound to plasma protein
drugs.precautions: Hypotension, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease. Hypertension tachycardia. Urinary retention or bladder dysfunction. Monitor growth in children, QT interval prolongation, history of seizures, susceptibility to angle-closure glaucoma, hepatic impairment, suicidal ideation. Pregnancy and lactation
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Generally reserve for ADHD patients who do not respond to, or are intolerant of, psychostimulants.
  • Give as a single dose in the morning or as 2 doses (in the morning and late afternoon).
  • Maximum of 1.4 mg/kg (not to exceed 100 mg) daily. Avoid maximum dose in people with moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment or taking potent CYP2D6 inhibitors like fluoxetine and paroxetine.
  • This medicine may make you feel drowsy or dizzy; do not drive or operate machinery if you are affected.

British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Following reports of suicidal thoughts and behavior, patients and their carers should be informed about the risk and told to report clinical worsening, suicidal thoughts or behavior, irritability, agitation or depression.
  • Following rare reports of hepatic disorders, patients and carers should be advised of the risk and be told how to recognize symptoms; prompt medical attention should be sought in case of abdominal pain, unexplained nausea, malaise, darkening of the urine, or jaundice.

drugs.indications:
To delay imminent preterm birth in pregnant women with:
i) Regular uterine contractions of at least 30 seconds duration at a rate of ≥4 per 30 minutes
ii) A cervical dilation of 1 to 3 cm (0-3 nulliparas) and effacement of ≥50%
iii) Age ≥18 years
iv) A gestational age from 28 until 33 completed weeks
v) A normal fetal heart rate.
drugs.dosages: Initial intravenous bolus dose of 6.75 mg (as 7.5 mg/ml solution), immediately followed by a continuous loading intravenous infusion at 18 mg/hr for 3 hours and then followed by intravenous infusion at 6 mg/hr up to 45 hours. The total duration of treatment should not exceed 48 hours and the total dose per treatment course should not exceed 330 mg of the active substance. The dosing is individualized according to product insert/protocol.
drugs.adverseReactions: Nausea & vomiting, headache, dizziness, hot flushes, tachycardia, hypotension, injection site reactions, hyperglycemia, fever, insomnia, itch, rash, allergic reaction, postpartum bleeding
drugs.contraindications: Gestational age below 28 or over 33 completed wk, premature rupture of the membranes after 30 wk of pregnancy, intrauterine growth retardation or abnormal fetal heart rate, antepartum uterine hemorrhage that requires immediate delivery, eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia requiring delivery, intrauterine fetal death, suspected intrauterine infection, placenta praevia, abruptio placenta, abnormal or high-risk pregnancy, known hypersensitivity to active substance or excipients.
drugs.interactions: It is unlikely that atosiban is involved in cytochrome P-450 mediated drug-drug interactions, as in vitro investigations have shown that atosiban is not a substrate for the cytochrome P-450 system and does not inhibit the drug metabolizing cytochrome P-450 enzymes. No clinically relevant interactions observed.
drugs.precautions: Renal & hepatic dysfunction, abnormally positioned placenta, multiple pregnancy or pregnancy between 24-27 wk, small for gestational age fetus. Treatment may be repeated up to 3 more times with uterine contractions & fetal heart rate monitored during use. May cause postpartum bleeding.

drugs.genericName: Atovaquone 250 mg and Proguanil 100 mg Tablet
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Prophylaxis of malaria
    • Start 1-2 days before entering and continue taking atovaquone with proguanil until 7 days after leaving an endemic area.
    • Adult, child >40 kg, 1 tablet once daily.
  • Treatment of uncomplicated malaria
    • Tablets must be taken for 3 days. Give with primaquine or tafenoquine for P. vivax or P. ovale malaria.
    • Adult, child >40 kg, 4 tablets once daily.
    • 30-40 kg, 3 tablets once daily.
    • 20-30 kg, 2 tablets once daily.
    • 10-20 kg, 1 tablet once daily.
  • Contraindicated for prophylaxis if CrCl <30 ml/minute (due to proguanil component); consider using an alternative antimalarial. Renal impairment increases the risk of blood dyscrasias.
  • This medicine is absorbed best if taken with food.
  • If necessary, crush the tablets and mix them with a small amount of milk (otherwise, swallow them whole).
  • Avoid mosquito bites by using repellents and wearing protective clothing.
  • People with a genetic lack of CYP2C19 activity cannot metabolise proguanil to cycloguanil, the active metabolite, however, it is uncertain if its prophylactic effect is reduced.

drugs.genericName: Atracurium Besilate 10 mg/ml in 2.5 ml Injection
drugs.indications: Muscle relaxant in general anesthesia, Endotracheal intubation, Aid controlled ventilation.
drugs.dosages: Adult & children >2 mth, 0.3-0.6 mg/kg IV. Endotracheal intubation dose: 0.5-0.6 mg/kg. Supplementary dose: 0.1-0.2 mg/kg as required. Continuous infusion rates of 0.3-0.6 mg/kg/hr to maintain neuromuscular block during long surgical procedure.
drugs.adverseReactions: Cutaneous reactions; bradycardia, transient hypotension in patients with CVS disorders; dyspnea, bronchospasm; rash and urticaria.
drugs.contraindications: Known allergic hypersensitivity to Atracurium besylate.
drugs.interactions: Mixed block with suxamethonium which is difficult to reverse with anticholinergic drugs. Ketamine may potentiate the effects of atracurium. Concurrent use with tamoxifen or danazol may prolong effects of atracurium. Neuromuscular blockade potentiated by parenteral Magnesium salts, anesthetics, aminoglycosides and polypeptide antibiotics, botulinum A toxin. Malignant hyperthermia with halogenated anesthetics and succinylcholine. MAOIs.
drugs.precautions: Neonates, severe CVS disorders, renal or hepatic dysfunction, myasthenia gravis and other neuromuscular disorders, severe electrolyte imbalances, respiratory insufficiency or pulmonary disease, asthma, burns, cardiopulmonary bypass, smoking, pregnancy and lactation. Atracurium should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit to the mother outweighs any potential risk to the fetus. Dosage for obese patients should be based on ideal body-weight to prevent overdosing.
drugs.notes:
MIMS, 2022 - Tracrium

  • Store at temperatures between 2°C and 8°C. Do not freeze. Protect from light.
  • Short periods at temperatures up to 25°C are permissible but ONLY to allow transportation or temporary storage outside of a cold store. It is estimated that a 5% loss of potency would occur if TRACRIUM injection was stored at 25°C for one month.
  • Any unused TRACRIUM injection from opened ampoules should be discarded.

MIMS, 2022 - Notrixum

  • Store at cold room (2-8°C) to preserve potency. Do not freeze.
  • Upon removal from refrigerator to room temperature storage conditions (below 30°C), use Notrixum injection within 14 days even if refrigerated.

i) Reduce vagal inhibition, salivary and bronchial secretion in anesthesia

iii) Reversal of effect of competitive muscle relaxants
iv) Overdosage with other compounds having muscarinic action
v) Organophosphate poisoning
drugs.dosages:
i) Adult, 300-600 mcg IM/SC 30-60 minutes before anesthesia. Alternatively, 300-600 mcg IV immediately before induction of anesthesia. Child: >20 kg, 300-600 mcg; 12-16 kg, 300 mcg; 7-9 kg, 200 mcg; >3 kg, 100 mcg. Doses to be given via IM/SC admin 30-60 minutes before anesthesia.
ii) Adult, 500 mcg every 3-5 minutes. Total: 3 mg. Max Dosage: 0.04 mg/kg body weight.
iii) Adult, 0.6-1.2 mg before or with anticholinesterase
iv) Adult, 0.6-1 mg IV/IM/SC, repeated every 2 hr.
v) Adult, 2 mg IV/IM, every 10-30 minutes until muscarinic effects disappear or atropine toxicity appears. In severe cases, dose can be given as often as every 5 minutes. In moderate to severe poisoning, a state of atropinisation is maintained for at least 2 days and continued for as long as symptoms are present. Child, 20 mcg/kg given every 5-10 minutes.
drugs.adverseReactions: Dry mouth, dysphagia, constipation, flushing and dryness of skin, tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias, mydriasis, photophobia, cycloplegia, raised intraocular pressure. Toxic doses cause tachycardia, hyperpyrexia, restlessness, confusion, excitement, hallucinations, delirium and may progress to circulatory failure and respiratory depression. Potentially Fatal: Atrial arrhythmias, AV dissociation, multiple ventricular ectopi.
drugs.contraindications: Glaucoma, chronic respiratory disease, sick sinus syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, cardiac failure, pyloric stenosis, prostatic hypertrophy.
drugs.interactions: Additive anticholinergic effects with quinidine, antidepressants and some antihistamines.
drugs.precautions: Reflux esophagitis, elderly, infants and children. Pregnancy.

    • Atropine is ineffective in heart transplant recipients due to lack of vagal innervation and likely not effective for type II second-degree or third-degree atrioventricular node block.
    • Adult, IV or IM, 0.5 to 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes; 1 mg is preferred for severe bradyarrhythmias (e.g. hypotension/shock, altered mental status, acute heart failure); maximum total dose: 3 mg.

  • Organophosphate poisoning
    • IV bolus
      • IV bolus 1mg with dose doubled every 3-5 minutes until clearing of respiratory secretions and bradycardia OR airway has been secured. For severe toxicity, intubation will usually be required concurrently to secure the airway and assist ventilation.
    • Infusion
      • Once patient has been intubated an infusion of 5-10 mg per hour can be instituted depending on severity of symptoms.
      • Or TOXINZ (child and adults): 0.02 to 0.08 mg/kg/hour IV. Titrate against response (doses of 0.5 to 2.4 mg/kg/hour have been used). Once secretions are dried, maintain with an infusion of 0.5-1 mg per hour to control secretions while carefully monitoring for signs of atropine toxicity. Atropine should be discontinued once patient shows signs of atropine toxicity or clinical improvement.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Diagnostic use
    • Adult, 1 eye drop (single dose) or 1 drop twice daily for 1-3 days before examination.
    • Child >1 year, usually 1 eye drop once daily for 1-3 days before examination.
  • Uveitis
    • Adult, 1 eye drop once or twice daily (maximum 4 times daily).
    • Child >2 years, 1 eye drop once daily. If inadequate, consider alternative treatment rather than increasing dose.
  • Postoperative use
    • Adult, 1 eye drop once or twice daily (maximum 4 times daily).

  • Enlarged pupils cause blurred vision and sensitivity to bright light; wearing dark glasses may help. Your ability to judge distance may be impaired. Do not drive or operate machinery while vision is disturbed.

Lexicomp, 2024

  • Palliative care of respiratory secretions (off-label use)
    • Adult, sublingual (using 1% ophthalmic solution): Initial: 1 to 2 drops every 2 to 4 hours; usual dose range: 2 to 4 drops every 2 to 4 hours.

    • Wash hands before and after use. Avoid touching tip of applicator to eye or other surfaces. Finger pressure should be applied to lacrimal sac for 1 to 3 minutes after instillation to decrease risk of absorption and systemic reactions.

British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Antimuscarinics dilate the pupil and paralyse the ciliary muscle; they vary in potency and duration of action.

  • Phenylephrine hydrochloride is a sympathomimetic licensed for mydriasis in diagnostic or therapeutic procedures. Mydriasis occurs within 60-90 minutes and lasts up to 5-7 hours.
  • Mydriatics and cycloplegics are used in the treatment of anterior uveitis, usually as an adjunct to corticosteroids. Atropine sulfate or cyclopentolate hydrochloride can prevent posterior synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm when used for anterior uveitis.

drugs.adverseReactions: Pneumonia, nasopharyngitis, febrile neutropenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, anorexia, dizziness, headache, dyspnea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, nausea, abdominal pain, petechiae, pruritis, rash, ecchymosis, arthralgia, fatigue, pyrexia, chest pain, injection site erythema, injection site pain, injection site reaction. drugs.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients. Advanced malignant hepatic tumors and lactation.
drugs.interactions: Based on in vitro data, azacitidine metabolism does not appear to be mediated by cytochrome P450 isoenzymes (CYPs), UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs), sulfotransferases (SULTs), and glutathione transferases (GSTs); interactions related to these metabolizing enzymes in vivo are therefore considered unlikely. Clinically significant inhibitory or inductive effects of azacitidine on cytochrome P450 enzymes are unlikely
drugs.precautions: Patients should be advised to promptly report febrile episodes. Patients and physicians are also advised to be observant for signs and symptoms of bleeding. Its also contraindicated in patients with advanced malignant hepatic tumor. Patients with renal impairment should be closely monitored for toxicity since azacitidine and/or its metabolites are primarily excreted by the kidney. NPRA Safety Alert (19 April 2023): Differentiation syndrome.
