Frank Shann Drug Doses, 2017

  • 10-20 mg/kg (adult, 0.5-1 g) 8H IV over 5-30 min. Severe inftn: 20-40 mg/kg (adult, 1-2 g) 12H (1st wk life) 8H (>1 wk) or constant infsn.

Lexidrug, 2026

  • General dosing, susceptible infection (non-CNS)
    • Infants, children and adolescents, IV: 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours; maximum dose: 1000 mg/dose; extended infusions may be needed for infections due to isolates with elevated MICs or in patients with critical illness.
  • Meningitis
    • Infants (limited data available in infants <3 months of age), children and adolescents, IV: 40 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours; maximum dose: 2000 mg/dose; duration should be individualized based on patient characteristics and response; treatment duration for gram-negative bacilli is a minimum of 10 to 14 days; although some experts recommend ≥21 days and at least 14 days after first negative cerebrospinal fluid culture.
  • Usual dosage range:
    • Traditional intermittent infusion method (over 30 minutes): Adult, IV: 500 mg every 6 hours or 1 to 2 g every 8 hours; 500 mg every 6 hours achieves comparable pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters to 1 g every 8 hours.
    • Extended infusion method (off-label): Adult, IV: 1 to 2 g every 8 hours over 3 hours. May give a loading dose of 1 to 2 g over 30 minutes, especially when rapid attainment of therapeutic drug concentrations is desired (e.g., sepsis). Some experts recommend 2 g every 8 hours over 3 hours for treatment of infections caused by certain resistant organisms (e.g., carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales).
    • Continuous infusion method (off-label): Adult, IV: 2 g every 8 hours over 8 hours or 3 g every 12 hours over 12 hours. May give a loading dose of 1 to 2 g over 30 minutes, especially when rapid attainment of therapeutic drug concentrations is desired (e.g., sepsis).

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Empirical treatment of nosocomial infections and life-threatening infections (when other antibacterials are inappropriate or contraindicated), or when multi-resistant Gram-negative infections are suspected or proven
    • Adult, IV 0.5-1 g every 8 hours. Maximum 2 g every 8 hours.
    • Child, IV 10 mg/kg (maximum 500 mg) every 8 hours; in more serious infections, use 20 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) every 8 hours.
  • Renal impairment, adult
    • CrCl 26-50 ml/minute, IV, chosen dose every 12 hours.
    • CrCl 10-25 ml/minute, IV, half the chosen dose every 12 hours.
    • CrCl <10 ml/minute, IV, half the chosen dose every 24 hours.
  • Exacerbation of lower respiratory tract infection in cystic fibrosis
    • Adult, IV 1-2 g every 8 hours.
    • Child, IV 40 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours.
  • Febrile neutropenia
    • Adult, IV 1-2 g every 8 hours.
  • Meningitis
    • Adult, IV 2 g every 8 hours.
    • Child, IV 40 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours.
  • Melioidosis
    • Adult, IV 1 g every 8 hours; for neurological melioidosis, use 2 g every 8 hours.
    • Child, IV 25 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) every 8 hours; for neurological melioidosis, use 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours.
  • Carbapenems have the broadest spectrum of all the antibacterial classes, with good activity against Gram-negative and Gram-positive organisms and anaerobes. They are resistant to hydrolysis by most beta-lactamases including extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), however, Gram-negative organisms with acquired ability to produce metallo-beta-lactamases (carbapenemases) often inactivate all beta-lactams except aztreonam.
  • All are inactive against MRSA, Enterococcus faecium and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Carbapenem resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii is increasing worldwide. Ertapenem is inactive against P. aeruginosa and Acinetobacter. Further resistance can develop during treatment.
  • Imipenem is given with cilastatin to prevent its inactivation by renal dehydropeptidase I.
  • Meropenem is effective in treating meningitis. Imipenem is contraindicated in meningitis due to its epileptogenic potential; however, if it is used carefully the difference in this potential between imipenem and meropenem is small. Ertapenem is also associated with seizures and there are no data regarding its use in meningitis.
  • Ertapenem is given once daily, imipenem is given every 6 hours and meropenem every 8 hours.

drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Ulcerative colitis, adult
    • Acute
      • Mezavant®: >18 years, 2.4-4.8 g once daily.
      • Pentasa®: up to 4 g daily in 1-4 doses, according to response.
      • Salofalk®: 1.5-3 g daily in 1-3 doses.
    • Maintenance
      • Mezavant®: >18 years, 2.4 g once daily.
      • Pentasa®: initially 1.5-2 g daily in 2 or 3 doses or 2 g once daily, according to response.
      • Salofalk®: 1.5 g daily in 1-3 doses.
  • Ulcerative colitis, child
    • Acute
      • Pentasa®: >5 years, 15-20 mg/kg 3 times daily.
      • Salofalk®: >6 years and <40 kg, 30-50 mg/kg daily in 1-3 doses.
    • Maintenance
      • Pentasa®: >5 years, 10 mg/kg 2-3 times daily.
      • Salofalk®: >6 years and <40 kg, 15-30 mg/kg daily in 1-3 doses.
  • Crohn's disease, adult
    • Acute
      • Pentasa®: up to 4 g daily in divided doses, according to response.
      • Salofalk®: 3-4.5 g daily in 1-3 doses.
    • Maintenance
      • Pentasa®: up to 4 g daily in divided doses, according to response.
      • Salofalk®: 1.5-3 g daily in 1-3 doses.
  • Swallow tablets or granules whole without chewing or crushing them.
    • Mesasal®: take tablets at least half an hour before food.
    • Mezavant®: take tablets with food.
    • Salofalk®: take tablets at least one hour before food; it doesn't matter when granules are taken in relation to food.
    • Pentasa®: it doesn't matter when the tablets or granules are taken in relation to food. The tablets may be dispersed in 50 ml cold water, stirred and taken immediately.
  • Different brands of mesalazine are not interchangeable due to differences in formulation and release characteristics.

Product leaflet, accessed 2025

  • Pentasa prolonged release granules sachet must not be chewed. The contents of the sachet should be emptied onto the tongue and washed down with some water or juice. Alternatively, the entire content of the sachet can be taken with yoghurt and consumed immediately.

British National Formulary 90, 2025

  • There is no evidence to show that any one oral preparation of mesalazine is more effective than another; however, the delivery characteristics of oral mesalazine preparations may vary.

drugs.genericName: Metformin 500 mg and Glibenclamide 2.5 mg Tablet
drugs.prescriberCategory: DELISTED FROM MOHMF 2019-2 because of the risk of hypoglycemia especially in the elderly and sufficient alternatives are available in the MOHMF.
drugs.indications: As second-line therapy when diet, exercise and initial treatment with sulphonylurea or metformin do not result in adequate glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus
drugs.dosages: Initial dose, 1.25 mg/250 mg ORALLY once daily; titrate in increments of 1.25 mg/250 mg per day every 2 weeks, 2.5 mg/500 mg to 5 mg/500 mg ORALLY twice daily; titrate in increments of 5 mg/500 mg up to MAX 20 mg/2000 mg once daily
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, cobalamin deficiency, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, dizziness
drugs.contraindications: Renal disease or renal dysfunction, chronic heart failure requiring pharmacologic treatment, acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis with or without coma, hypersensitivity to metformin or glibenclamide
drugs.interactions: Cationic drugs that are eliminated by renal tubular secretion. Thiazide and other diuretics, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid products, estrogens, oral contraceptives, phenytoin, nicotinic acid, sympathomimetics, calcium channel blockers and isoniazid may produce hyperglycemia and lead to loss of glycemic control. drugs.precautions: Adrenal or pituitary insufficiency elderly, debilitated or malnourished patients, excessive alcohol intake, hypoxic states due to shock, acute chronic heart failure or acute myocardial infarction, lactic acidosis, severe metabolic complication due to accumulation of metformin, liver or renal disease, peripheral vascular disease, pulmonary disease, pregnancy or lactation, stress caused by infection, fever, trauma or surgery
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Type 2 diabetes
    • Adult, initially 1 tablet of 500 mg metformin with 2.5 mg glibenclamide daily with breakfast. Increase by 1 tablet (of this strength) every 2 weeks or longer according to response. Maximum dose, 1 tablet of 500 mg metformin with 5 mg glibenclamide 3 times a day.
    • Elderly, avoid use (risk of hypoglycemia and dose titration may be difficult).
  • Make sure that you, and your friends and family, know how to recognise and treat hypoglycaemia (low blood glucose); ask your doctor or diabetes educator if you are unsure.
  • Monitor blood glucose when switching from standard tablets to fixed-dose combination because tablets are not bioequivalent. Do not use the previous doses of metformin and glibenclamide to start fixed-dose combination therapy.

drugs.genericName: Metformin HCl 1000 mg Extended Release Tablet
drugs.brandName: Glucophage XR, Diabetmin XR, Glucient XR, Melifort, Metswift XR
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 86, 2023

  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus [monotherapy or in combination with other antidiabetic drugs (including insulin)]
    • Adult, initially 500 mg once daily, then increased if necessary up to 2 g once daily, dose increased gradually, every 10-15 days, dose to be taken with evening meal, alternatively increased to 1 g twice daily, dose to be taken with meals, alternative dose only to be used if control not achieved with once daily dose regimen. If control still not achieved then change to standard release tablet.
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus [reduction in risk or delay of onset]
    • Adult 18-74 years, initially 500 mg once daily, then increase if necessary up to 2 g once daily, dose increased gradually, every 10-15 days, dose to be taken with evening meal, for further information on risk factors - consult product literature.
  • A European review, with input from the MHRA, has found vitamin B12 deficiency to be a common side-effect in patients treated with metformin, especially in those receiving a higher dose or longer treatment duration and in those with risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Take with or after food to reduce stomach upset.
  • Swallow controlled release tablets whole; do not chew or crush them.
  • Compliance with treatment is most important, so be guided by convenience for the patient when advising when to take the dose of controlled release metformin; if GI adverse effects are a problem with morning administration consider giving with the evening meal.
  • Increase dosage slowly to limit GI adverse effects; reduce or stop treatment if symptoms persist.
  • Drinking alcohol can affect control of your diabetes. It can also increase the risk of serious side effects. Limit your alcohol intake, avoid binge drinking and have something to eat when you drink alcohol.
  • Slow onset of effect; control may take up to 2 weeks to establish.
  • Metformin has rarely been associated with lactic acidosis. Phenformin (a related biguanide) was withdrawn from the market due to its association with severe lactic acidosis and there was concern that metformin might have the same risk. A causal relationship with metformin is not established and epidemiological data suggest that the incidence of lactic acidosis in metformin-treated diabetics is not higher than in patients on other treatments.
  • Pregnancy: Usually replaced with insulin; seek specialist advice. There is some clinical experience and metformin appears safe (however, long-term follow-up of children exposed in utero is limited).

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2021

  • Signs or symptoms of lactic acidosis include acidosis, nausea, vomiting, increased respiratory rate, abdominal pain, shock, and tachycardia.
  • Historically contraindicated if SCr 1.5 mg/dL or greater in men and 1.4 mg/dL or greater in women or reduced creatinine clearance (CrCl). In 2016, the FDA suggested that eGFR be used as a measure of kidney function rather than creatinine alone. Discontinue if eGFR is less than 30 ml/minute/m2, and initiating if eGFR is 30-45 ml/minute/m2 is not recommended. Assess benefit of continuing use in patients already prescribed metformin if eGFR is 30-45 ml/minute/1.73 m2 and consider a 50% dose reduction. Monitor renal function every 3-6 months in patients with eGFR of 45-60 ml/minute/1.73 m2 and every 3 months if 30-45 ml/minute/1.73 m2.

drugs.indications: Detoxification treatment or maintenance treatment of narcotic addiction.
drugs.dosages: Initial 10-20 mg per day, increasing by 10-20 mg per day until there are no signs of withdrawal or intoxication. Usual dose 40-60 mg/day
drugs.adverseReactions: Constipation, nausea, vomiting, asthenia, dizziness, somnolence, cardiac arrest, disease of cardiovascular system, shock, respiratory arrest, respiratory depression, diaphoresis, constipation, sedation. NPRA Safety Alert (2 November 2022): Hypoglycemia.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to methadone, severe hepatic impairment, respiratory depression, obstructive airways disease, ulcerative colitis, concomitant administration with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 2 weeks of discontinuation
drugs.interactions: Buprenorphine, didanosine, efavirenz, fluconazole, fluvoxamine, naltrexone, nevirapine, rifampin, risperidone, ritonavir, voriconazole, zidovudine
drugs.precautions: May cause dependence on prolonged use. Avoid alcoholic beverages, effects on ability to drive or operate machine. Methadone, even in low doses is a special hazard for children, non-dependent adults are also at risk of toxicity and dependent adults are at risk if tolerance is incorrectly assessed during induction. NPRA Safety Alert (22 Jan 2026): Risk of Oesophageal Dysfunction.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • It takes a few days to gain the full effect of a dose of methadone. In the meantime, you may feel uncomfortable but should not take opioids, alcohol or benzodiazepines as this increases the risk of overdose, can affect assessment of your symptoms, and it will take longer to tailor your dose.
    • Methadone's long half-life (24-36 hours) means that it takes up to 5 days to reach steady-state concentrations for a particular dose.
    • Assess patients daily for at least the first 5 days of methadone maintenance for signs of withdrawal or intoxication and adjust dose accordingly (fatal drug toxicity is most common in the first 2 weeks).
  • Methadone may cause drowsiness particularly when starting treatment or if the dose is increased; do not drive or operate machinery if you are affected.
    • Tolerance develops to methadone's sedative effects (after 4-6 weeks), enabling normal activities (e.g. employment, education) to be resumed; encourage patients to continue treatment for at least 18-24 months.
  • Tell any doctor or dentist who is treating you that you are on the methadone program so they can prescribe appropriately.
  • If someone on methadone maintenance has a painful condition requiring opioid analgesics, higher than standard doses may be needed for pain relief (in addition to regular methadone).

Micromedex, 2024

  • Side effects may include nausea, vomiting, sweating, lightheadedness, asthenia, dizziness or sedation.
  • Tell patient to report symptoms of severe constipation, respiratory depression, adrenal insufficiency, severe hypotension or an arrhythmia.
  • Advise patient against sudden discontinuation of drug due to potential for withdrawal symptoms.

drugs.indications:
i) Solid tumors
ii) Gestational trophoblastic disease
iii) Acute leukemias, lymphomas
drugs.dosages:
i) 50 mg/m2 once every 3 weeks in combination with other drugs (for this dose, use the 50 mg preparation)
ii) 50 mg IV Day 1, 3, 5, 9 every 3 weeks. For high risk gestational trophoblastic disease, use 100 mg/m2 as part of EMA-CO regime
iii) High dose regimes: 500-3000 mg/m2 per dose may be used, employing the 500 mg preparations. Child: Central nervous system prophylaxis for acute leukemia 2 gm/m2 over 24 hours with folinic acid rescue, 3 doses for B-cell lineage. 4 doses for T-lineage all every 3 weeks. Relapse acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL): 1 gm/m2 over 36 hours with folinic acid rescue every 3 weeks for 9 doses, maintenance: 50 mg/m2 every 2 weeks. B-cell lymphoma: 3 gm/m2 over 3 hours with folinic acid rescue for three doses. Methotrexate level monitoring recommended when using high dose regimens.

THE 500 MG STRENGTH IS NOT FOR INTRATHECAL USE
drugs.adverseReactions: Myelosuppression, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, transient abnormalities in serum levels of liver enzymes, acute hepatocellular injury (not common at standard dose), erythematous rash, pruritis, pigmentary changes, photosensitivity, acute renal failure (high dose), headache, drowsiness, dizziness, acute confusion (high dose), interstitial pneumonitis, myelosuppression, interstitial pneumonitis. NPRA Safety Alert (13 June 2018): Risk of Pulmonary Alveolar Hemorrhage.
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, lactation, severe myelosuppression, serious renal and liver impairment, increase risk of toxicity in the presence of third space fluid (pleural effusion, ascites).
drugs.interactions: Alcohol, aminophenazone, amiodarone, amitriptyline, antibiotics, cisplatinum, ciclosporin, cytosine arabinoside, diclofenac, etoposide, etretinate, 5-fluorouracil, NSAIDs, salicylates, nephrotoxic drugs, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, teniposide, warfarin, folic acid. NPRA Safety Alert (23 March 2018): Risk of drug interaction with levetiracetam.
drugs.precautions: Patients with a creatinine clearance of less than 60 ml/minute, impaired renal function, pleural effusion, ascitis or poor nutritional status should not receive high-dose methotrexate. High-dose or intrathecal methotrexate therapy must NOT be formulated with diluents containing preservatives. High-dose methotrexate therapy requires the use of leucovorin rescue. Myelosuppression, acute or chronic hepatotoxicity (elevated transaminases, fibrosis, cirrhosis), pulmonary toxicity (dry cough, pneumonitis). Women of child-bearing potential, gastrointestinal toxicity (vomiting, diarrhea, stomatitis), tumor lysis syndrome in patients with rapidly growing tumors, severe and sometimes fatal skin reactions, potentially fatal infections (especially Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia), neurotoxicity (leukoencephalopathy, seizures), care should be taken in handling the body fluids of persons receiving antineoplastic agents.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Injection is yellow.
  • Tell your doctor if you have nausea, mouth ulcers, bruising, diarrhea or signs of infection.
  • Tell your doctor and pharmacist that you are taking methotrexate before starting any new medicines.
  • Avoid excessive or prolonged sun exposure, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen.
  • Ensure effective contraception during treatment. Stop methotrexate for >3 months before conception and give folate supplement, e.g. folic acid 5 mg daily, and continue during first trimester.
  • Myelosuppression is usually low grade with calcium folinate rescue. If methotrexate clearance is prolonged or calcium folinate rescue administration is delayed, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and/or anemia may occur and can be severe. Neutrophil and platelet nadirs occur about 5-13 days after a bolus dose with recovery at 14-28 days. Neutropenia may be biphasic with the first nadir 4-7 days after a dose and the second at 12-21 days.
  • Hepatotoxicity: Increased aminotransferases are common and usually transient and asymptomatic. Fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver failure are rare.
  • High-dose methotrexate
    • Calcium folinate rescue is required for methotrexate doses >100 mg/m2, refer to treatment protocols.
    • High-dose treatment (e.g. >1 g/m2) requires slow infusion, hydration and alkalinisation of urine to prevent renal failure associated with crystal formation, refer to treatment protocols.
  • Monitor patients for symptoms of pneumonitis; if suspected, exclude pneumonia, withdraw methotrexate and give corticosteroids.

British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Maintenance of remission of severe Crohn's disease (under expert supervision)
    • Adult, 10-25 mg once weekly.
  • Moderate to severe active rheumatoid arthritis (under expert supervision)
    • Adult, 7.5 mg once weekly, adjusted according to response; maximum 20 mg per week.
  • Severe psoriasis unresponsive to conventional therapy (under expert supervision)
    • Adult, initially 2.5-10 mg once weekly, then increased in steps of 2.5-5 mg, adjusted according to response, dose to be adjusted at intervals of at least 1 week; usual dose 7.5-15 mg once weekly, stop treatment if inadequate response after 3 months at the optimum dose; maximum 30 mg per week.

  • Patients and their carers should be advised to avoid exposure to UV light (including intense sunlight, sunlamps and sunbeds).

Lexicomp, 2020

  • Uveitis (off-label use)
    • Adult, 7.5 mg to 20 mg once weekly either alone or in conjunction with other corticosteroids/ immunosuppressants.

  • Morphea or localized scleroderma (off-label use)
    • For use in patients with severe skin and/or musculoskeletal involvement, either as monotherapy or in combination with glucocorticoids.

  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (adjunctive agent) (off-label use)
    • For use in patients with arthritis-predominant disease who require glucocorticoid-sparing therapy, or in patients with persistent arthritis symptoms despite first-line therapy.
    • Adult, initial: 5 to 15 mg once weekly (in combination with folic acid). Increase dose gradually (e.g., by 2.5 mg/week every 4 weeks) if needed based on response (maximum: 20 to 25 mg/week).
  • Methotrexate peak serum levels may be decreased if taken with food. Management: Administer without regard to food.

  • Take this medication strictly as directed. It should be taken once a week on the same day each week; it must not be taken every day.

  • Do not sunbathe for 24 hours before, and 48 hours after, PUVA therapy.
  • After taking oral methoxsalen, avoid exposure to sunlight, even through glass and cloud cover, for at least 8 hours. After application to the skin, avoid exposure of treated areas to sunlight for at least 12-48 hours. If exposure to sunlight cannot be avoided, protective clothing should be worn and sunscreens applied to all areas that may be exposed, including lips.
  • Wear wrap-around sunglasses with 100% UVA-absorbing properties during daylight (even on a cloudy day or if exposed to sunlight through a window) for 24 hours after taking oral methoxsalen to avoid cataracts.
  • Some foods contain natural photosensitisers, e.g. limes, figs, parsley, parsnips, mustard, carrots and celery; avoid eating large amounts of these foods while using methoxsalen.
  • PUVA treatments may be given 2 or 3 times a week, but must be at least 48 hours apart. Most people will require 20-30 PUVA treatments before psoriasis clears; treatment may be continued less frequently to keep psoriasis under control.
  • If nausea occurs, divide the oral dose in two and give 15 minutes apart.

drugs.indications: Protection before exposure to sunlight, psoriasis and vitiligo
drugs.dosages: 0.2-0.6 mg/kg/body weight. For repigmentation of larger lesions (greater than 6 cm sq), 20 mg/day 2 hours before exposure. Take with food or milk
drugs.adverseReactions: Erythema, pruritus, headache, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, skin pain, hepatotoxicity, precancerous changes
drugs.contraindications: History of idiosyncratic reactions to psoralens, history of light sensitive disease states (lupus erythematosus, porphyria cutanea tarda, erythropoietic protoporphyria, variegate porphyria, xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism). History of melanoma
drugs.interactions: Phenytoin may decreased methoxsalen effectiveness
drugs.precautions: Breast feeding, exposure to sunlight or UVA radiation, ocular changes, patients with a history of previous arsenic exposure should be observed for signs of carcinoma, patients with a history of previous radiation therapy or Grenz ray therapy should be observed
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2020

  • Psoriasis:
    • Initial: 10 to 70 mg 1.5 to 2 hours (Oxsoralen Ultra) or 2 hours (8-MOP) before exposure to UVA light; dose may be repeated 2-3 times per week, based on UVA exposure; doses must be given at least 48 hours apart; dosage is based upon patient's body weight and skin type:
      • <30 kg, 10 mg
      • 30 to 50 kg, 20 mg
      • 51 to 65 kg, 30 mg
      • 66 to 80 kg, 40 mg
      • 81 to 90 kg, 50 mg
      • 91 to 115 kg, 60 mg
      • >115 kg, 70 mg
      • Note: Dosage may be increased (one time) by 10 mg after 15th treatment if minimal or no response.
    • Maintenance: When 95% psoriasis clearing achieved, may begin 1 treatment every week for at least 2 treatments; followed by 1 treatment every 2 weeks for at least 2 treatments; then every 3 weeks for at least 2 treatments then as needed to maintain response while minimizing UVA exposure.
  • To reduce nausea, capsules should be administered with food or milk.

drugs.genericName: Methoxy Polyethylene Glycol-epoetin Beta 100 mcg/0.3 ml Injection in Prefilled Syringe
drugs.indications: Treatment of anemia associated with chronic renal failure.
drugs.prescribingRestrictions: Patients who require higher doses of erythropoietin if it is more cost saving to use a long-acting agent instead of short-acting agents.
drugs.dosages: Non Erythropoiesis Stimulating Agent (ESA)-treated patients, 0.6 mcg/kg, once every two weeks (IV or SC). When the Hb is >11 g/dl, administration can be reduced to once monthly using the dose equal to twice the previous two weekly dose. ESA-treated patients, 120-360 mcg once monthly or 60-180 mcg every two weeks.
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypertension, vascular access thrombosis, headache, hypersensitivity, hypertensive encephalopathy and rash (rare). Increased risk of mortality and/or tumor progression and Pure Red Cell Aplasia.
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, known hypersensitivity to the active substance or any of the excipients.
drugs.interactions: No interaction studies have been performed
drugs.precautions: Uncontrolled hypertension. Evaluate iron status prior to and during treatment to determine whether supplementary iron is necessary. Discontinue if Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) is diagnosed. May stimulate growth of any type of malignancy. Pregnancy and lactation. Not recommended for patients < 18 years.
drugs.notes:
MIMS, 2022

  • Store in the refrigerator at 2°C to 8°C. Do not freeze.
  • Keep the pre-filled syringe in the outer carton in order to protect from light.
  • For pre-filled syringe: The patient may remove the product from refrigeration for storage at room temperature (not above 30°C) for one single period of 1 month. Once removed from the refrigerator the product must be used within this period.

drugs.notes:
Product leaflet, accessed 2024

  • For relief of aches and pains associated with muscle fatigue, muscle pain, backache, stiff shoulder, joint pain, strains, sprains, bruises and arthritis.
    • Adults and children 12 years of age and above, shake the can very well before use. To avoid frostbite, hold the can 10 cm away from the skin, and spray each affected area for no longer than 1 second. Apply to affected area not more than 3 to 4 times daily.
    • Children 2 to 12 years of age, consult a doctor.
  • Do not use
    • On wounds or damaged skin.
    • If you are allergic to any of the ingredients of this product.
    • Children under 2 years of age.

  • Alcohol: 87% w/w.

Product leaflet, accessed 2024

    • For sore muscles and back pain, work in before your exercise to warm up and after exercise to relieve muscle soreness and stiffness. Apply to affected area. Massage gently until absorbed into the skin. Repeat 3 to 4 times a day.
  • For external use only. Do not apply to wounds or damaged or very sensitive skin. Do not wrap, bandage or apply external heat or hot water.
  • This product contains Methyl Salicylate and when applied or rubbed onto the skin can be absorbed through the skin into the blood. For patients taking warfarin, excessive application onto the skin for muscle or joint pains may increase the chances of bleeding.
  • If pain persists for more than 10 days, or redness is present, or in conditions affecting children under 12 years of age, consult a physician immediately. Discontinue use if excessive irritation of the skin develops. Avoid getting into the eyes or mucous membranes.
  • Does not stain clothing or bed linen. Greaseless. Stainless.

drugs.indications: Hypertension
drugs.dosages: Adult, 250 mg 2-3 times daily, gradually increased at intervals of 2 or more days, maximum: 3 g/day. Elderly, initially 125 mg twice daily, increased gradually, maximum: 2 g daily. Child, initially, 10 mg/kg or 300 mg/m2 daily in 2-4 divided doses; increase as necessary. Max: 65 mg/kg, 2 g/m2 or 3 g daily, whichever is least.
drugs.adverseReactions: Sedation, headache, weakness, dizziness, parkinsonism, bradycardia, orthostatic hypotension, GI symptoms, hepatic impairment, impotence
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to methyldopa, history of hepatitis, autonomic dysfunction, bilateral cardiovascular disease
drugs.interactions: Antihypertensive drugs, lithium, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
drugs.precautions: Avoid abrupt withdrawal, congestive heart failure, dialysis patients (risk of hypertension following procedure), edema, hemolytic anemia, hypotension, liver disease, severe bilateral cerebrovascular disease (risk of choreoathetotic movements)
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine may make you feel drowsy or light-headed especially at the start of treatment or when the dose is increased; if affected, do not drive or operate machinery.
  • You may feel dizzy on standing when you first start taking this medicine or when the dose is increased. Get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimise this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy.
  • It is used to treat hypertension in pregnancy but CNS and hepatic adverse effects limit its use in other patients.
  • The sedating effect of methyldopa is exacerbated by dose increases; increase dosage at night to minimise inconvenience of increased sedation.
  • Monitor blood count and liver function during first 6-12 weeks of treatment.

Lexicomp, 2021

  • According to the World Health Organization (WHO), methyldopa is compatible with breastfeeding. However, because maternal depression has been reported following methyldopa administration, use of methyldopa should be avoided in the postnatal period due to the underlying risk of depression already present in this patient population.

drugs.indications:
i) For treatment of idiopathic and drug-induced methemoglobinemia
ii) As dye in diagnostic procedures
drugs.dosages:
i) Adult and children, 1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes. This dosage can be repeated if necessary after one hour.
ii) A dose of 5 mg/kg diluted in 500 ml of glucose 5% infused over 1 hour has been used successfully to stain and identify the parathyroid glands.

Dosing is individualized and according to product insert/protocol.
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypertension, hypotension, sweating symptom, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, confusion, cardiac dysrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to methylene blue, severe renal impairment, methemoglobinemia in cyanide poisoning, intraspinal injection, G6PD deficiency.
drugs.interactions: Not known
drugs.precautions: Hemolytic anemia (Heinz-body anemia) and hyperbilirubinemia in neonates who had been exposed to methylene blue in the amniotic cavity. Do NOT administer by subcutaneous or intrathecal injection, renal impairment.
drugs.notes:
Micromedex, 2021

drugs.indications:
i) Intramuscular administration: anti-inflammatory treatment, treatment of hematological and oncological disorders, endocrine disorders
ii) Intrasynovial, periarticular, intrabursal or soft tissue administration: Indicated as adjunctive therapy for short term administration in: Synovitis of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute and subacute bursitis, acute gouty arthritis, epicondylitis, acute nonspecific tenosynovitis, post-traumatic osteoarthritis
iii) Intralesional use in alopecia areata, discoid lupus erythematosus; keloids, localized hypertrophic, infiltrated inflammatory lesions of granuloma annulare, lichen planus, psoriatic plaques, lichen simplex chronicus (neurodermatitis) *Restricted to patients experiencing side effects with triamcinolone acetonide
drugs.dosages:
i. Intramuscular route a) Asthma: may be used in place of a short burst of oral steroids in vomiting or non-adherent patients. The recommended dose is 80-120 mg intramuscularly as a one-dose b) Adrenogenital syndrome: 40 mg every two weeks c) Rheumatoid arthritis (maintenance): 40-120 mg weekly d) Dermatologic lesions (acute severe dermatitis, chronic contact dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis): 40-120 mg weekly for 1-4 weeks
ii. Intraarticular route Recommended dose is 4 to 80 milligrams, depending upon the size of the joint. Injections may be repeated at intervals of 1 to 5 or more weeks in chronic cases
iii. Intralesional route 20 to 60 milligrams methylprednisolone acetate injected into the lesion
drugs.adverseReactions: Local atrophy, pigmentation changes, post-inj flare, sterile abscess, Charcot-like syndrome; Na & fluid retention; impaired wound healing, thin fragile skin; decreased carbohydrate tolerance; muscle weakness, myopathy, aseptic necrosis, tendon rupture; cataract, increased intraocular & intracranial pressure; growth retardation; psychic derangements.
drugs.contraindications: Systemic fungal infections, known hypersensitivity to components
drugs.interactions: Reduced efficacy with phenytoin, phenobarbitone, rifampicin. Corticosteroids may reduce effects of diuretics, hypoglycemics, anticholinesterases, salicylates.
drugs.precautions: Unusual stress, intercurrent infection; immunization (defer); active or latent TB; ocular herpes simplex; renal insufficiency, hypertension; osteoporosis; myasthenia gravis; pregnancy. Non-specific ulcerative colitis. Contains benzyl alcohol, which is potentially toxic when administered locally to neural tissue. Not for intrathecal. NPRA Safety Alert (19 July 2022): Pheochromocytoma crisis, which may be fatal, has been reported after administration of systemic corticosteroids. Corticosteroids should only be administered to patients with suspected or identified pheochromocytoma after an appropriate risk/benefit evaluation.

Corticosteroids should only be administered to patients with suspected or identified pheochromocytoma after an appropriate risk/benefit evaluation.

The maximum dose in 24 hours is 0.5 mg/kg body weight. Dosing table: Child age 1-3 years old (body weight 10-14 kg), 1 mg TDS; 3-5 years old (body weight 15-19 kg), 2 mg TDS; 5-9 years old (body weight 20-29 kg), 2.5 mg TDS; 9-18 years old (body weight 30-60 kg), 5 mg TDS; 15-18 years old (body weight >60 kg), 10 mg TDS. drugs.notes:
British National Formulary for Children 2025-2026, 2025

  • Second-line option for treatment of established postoperative nausea and vomiting
    • Child 1-17 years, 100-150 micrograms/kg up to 3 times a day (max. per dose 10 mg) for a maximum of 48 hours.
  • Second-line option for treatment of established postoperative nausea and vomiting; Second-line option for prevention of delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
    • Child 1-17 years, 100-150 micrograms/kg up to 3 times a day (max. per dose 10 mg) for a maximum of 5 days.

Lexidrug, 2026

  • Dyspepsia, functional (refractory) (off-label use)
    • For patients unresponsive to first-line therapies (e.g. proton pump inhibitors, Helicobacter pylori eradication, and/or tricyclic antidepressants); some experts recommend limiting duration of metoclopramide therapy to 4 weeks.
    • Adult, 5 to 10 mg 3 to 4 times daily administered prior to meals and at bedtime. A lower dose of 2 mg 3 times daily (using oral liquid formulation) may provide sufficient response.
  • Hiccups (alternative agent) (off-label use)
    • Limited data available. Treatment generally continues for up to 5 to 10 days. May discontinue treatment the day after hiccups subside; if hiccups recur, longer treatment duration may be needed (e.g. in palliative care).
    • Adult, 10 mg every 6 to 8 hours.
  • Gastroesophageal reflux, treatment
    • Routine use is not recommended; reserve use as a last resort after all other therapies have failed and following consultation with a GI specialist. Limited data available; efficacy results variable.
    • Infants, children and adolescents, 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg/dose every 6 to 8 hours; maximum dose: 10 mg/dose.
  • Tablets and oral solution: For scheduled dosing, administer 30 minutes prior to meals and at bedtime.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine may make you feel drowsy or dizzy; do not drive or operate machinery until you know how metoclopramide affects you.
  • Use short term only (maximum of 5 days); risk of tardive dyskinesia increases with cumulative dose and length of treatment.

British National Formulary 91, 2026

  • Metoclopramide can induce acute dystonic reactions involving facial and skeletal muscle spasms and oculogyric crises. These dystonic effects are more common in the young (especially girls and young women) and the very old; they usually occur shortly after starting treatment with metoclopramide and subside within 24 hours of stopping it. Injection of an antiparkinsonian drug such as procyclidine will abort dystonic attacks.

LactMed, 2026

  • Metoclopramide has no officially established dosage for increasing milk supply. Most studies have used metoclopramide in a dosage of 10 mg 2 or 3 times daily for 7 to 14 days. Some studies used a tapering dosage for the last days few of the regimen to avoid an abrupt drop in milk supply after drug discontinuation. No published literature supports the efficacy or safety of higher dosages, longer treatment periods or repeated courses of therapy.
  • Postpartum mothers are at a relatively high risk for postpartum depression and metoclopramide can cause depression as a side effect. Therefore, metoclopramide should probably be avoided in women with a history of major depression and not used for prolonged periods in any mothers during this time of high susceptibility.
  • Long-term uses of metoclopramide also increases the risk of tardive dyskinesia. Other reported side effects in nursing mothers include tiredness, nausea, headache, diarrhea, dry mouth, breast discomfort, vertigo, restless legs, intestinal gas, hair loss, irritability and anxiety.

drugs.adverseReactions: Lassitude, gastrointestinal and sleep pattern disturbances; rarely, non-specific skin reactions and coldness of extremities
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to metoprolol products, bradycardia, 2nd and 3rd degree AV block overt cardiac failure, cardiogenic shock, obstructive pulmonary disease
drugs.interactions: Alpha-1 adrenergic blockers, amiodarone, chlorpromazine, chlorprothixene, cimetidine, clonidine, digoxin, dihydropyridine, calcium channel blockers, flunarizine, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, hydralazine, hypoglycemic agents, lidocaine, methyldopa

drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Some beta-blockers are lipid soluble and some are water soluble. Water-soluble beta blockers (such as atenolol, celiprolol hydrochloride, nadolol, and sotalol hydrochloride) are less likely to enter the brain, and may therefore cause less sleep disturbance and nightmares. Water-soluble beta-blockers are excreted by the kidneys and dosage reduction is often necessary in renal impairment.
  • Beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm and should therefore usually be avoided in patients with a history of asthma. When there is no suitable alternative, it may be necessary for a patient with well-controlled asthma, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (without significant reversible airways obstruction), to receive treatment with a beta-blocker for a co-existing condition (e.g. heart failure or following myocardial infarction). In this situation, a cardioselective beta-blocker should be selected and initiated at a low dose by a specialist; the patient should be closely monitored for adverse effects. Atenolol, bisoprolol fumarate, metoprolol tartrate, nebivolol, and (to a lesser extent) acebutolol, have less effect on the beta2 (bronchial) receptors and are, therefore, relatively cardioselective, but they are not cardiospecific. They have a lesser effect on airways resistance but are not free of this side-effect.

Lexicomp, 2021

  • Food increases absorption. Metoprolol serum levels may be increased if taken with food. Management: Take immediate release tartrate tablets with food; extended release succinate can be taken with or without food.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine may cause dizziness or tiredness especially at the start of treatment or when the dose is increased; if affected, do not drive or operate machinery.
  • If you feel dizzy, get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimise this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy.
  • Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly unless your doctor tells you to.
  • When stopping treatment, reduce dosage gradually, e.g. over at least 2 weeks; avoid abrupt withdrawal as it may exacerbate angina, or precipitate rebound hypertension, MI or arrhythmias.

drugs.genericName: Metoprolol Tartrate 25 mg and Ivabradine 5 mg Tablet
drugs.notes:
Product leaflet, accessed 2022

  • Symptomatic treatment of chronic stable angina pectoris as substitution therapy in adult patients with normal sinus rhythm already controlled on metoprolol and ivabradine taken concomitantly at the same dose level.
    • Adult, one tablet twice daily, once in the morning and once in the evening.
  • Implicor should be taken orally twice daily during meals. The exposure of metoprolol is increased when administered with food. This should be considered in patients who currently take metoprolol in a fasting state and switch to Implicor.
  • It is recommended that the decision to titrate treatment takes place with the availability of serial heart measurements, ECG or ambulatory 24-hour monitoring and titration should be done with the individual components metoprolol and ivabradine, ensuring the patient is maintained at an optimal dose of metoprolol and ivabradine. If during treatment, heart rate decreases below 50 beats per minute at rest or the patient experiences symptoms related to bradycardia such as dizziness, fatigue or hypotension, down titration should be done with the individual monocomponents metoprolol and ivabradine, ensuring the patient is maintained at an optimal dose of metoprolol. After dose reduction, heart rate should be monitored. Treatment must be discontinued if heart rate remains below 50 bpm or symptoms of bradycardia persist despite dose reduction.
  • Should be used with precaution in patients with creatinine clearance below 15 ml/min.

drugs.adverseReactions: Lassitude, gastrointestinal and sleep pattern disturbances; rarely, non-specific skin reactions and coldness of extremities
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to metoprolol products, bradycardia, 2nd and 3rd degree AV block overt cardiac failure, cardiogenic shock, obstructive pulmonary disease
drugs.interactions: Alpha-1 adrenergic blockers, amiodarone, chlorpromazine, chlorprothixene, cimetidine, clonidine, digoxin, dihydropyridine, calcium channel blockers, flunarizine, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, hydralazine, hypoglycemic agents, lidocaine, methyldopa
drugs.precautions: Pregnancy, lactation
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Some beta-blockers are lipid soluble and some are water soluble. Water-soluble beta blockers (such as atenolol, celiprolol hydrochloride, nadolol, and sotalol hydrochloride) are less likely to enter the brain, and may therefore cause less sleep disturbance and nightmares. Water-soluble beta-blockers are excreted by the kidneys and dosage reduction is often necessary in renal impairment.
  • Beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm and should therefore usually be avoided in patients with a history of asthma. When there is no suitable alternative, it may be necessary for a patient with well-controlled asthma, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (without significant reversible airways obstruction), to receive treatment with a beta-blocker for a co-existing condition (e.g. heart failure or following myocardial infarction). In this situation, a cardioselective beta-blocker should be selected and initiated at a low dose by a specialist; the patient should be closely monitored for adverse effects. Atenolol, bisoprolol fumarate, metoprolol tartrate, nebivolol, and (to a lesser extent) acebutolol, have less effect on the beta2 (bronchial) receptors and are, therefore, relatively cardioselective, but they are not cardiospecific. They have a lesser effect on airways resistance but are not free of this side-effect.

Lexicomp, 2021

  • Food increases absorption. Metoprolol serum levels may be increased if taken with food. Management: Take immediate release tartrate tablets with food; extended release succinate can be taken with or without food.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine may cause dizziness or tiredness especially at the start of treatment or when the dose is increased; if affected, do not drive or operate machinery.
  • If you feel dizzy, get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimise this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy.
  • Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly unless your doctor tells you to.
  • When stopping treatment, reduce dosage gradually, e.g. over at least 2 weeks; avoid abrupt withdrawal as it may exacerbate angina, or precipitate rebound hypertension, MI or arrhythmias.

drugs.indications: Anaerobic infection
drugs.dosages:
Anaerobic infections: Adult, as a 1-g suppository 8 hrly for 3 days, then 12 hrly. Substitute oral therapy as soon as possible. May be unsuitable for initiating therapy in severe infections. Child: <1 yr, 125 mg; 1-5 yr, 250 mg; 5-10 yr, 500 mg. All doses to be given 8 hrly for 3 days, then 12 hrly thereafter. May be unsuitable for initiating therapy in severe infections.

Prophylaxis of postoperative anaerobic bacterial infections: Adult, 1 g 8 hrly starting 2 hr before surgery.
drugs.adverseReactions: GI disturbances e.g. nausea, unpleasant metallic taste, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation. Furred tongue, glossitis, and stomatitis due to overgrowth of Candida. Rarely, antibiotic-associated colitis. Weakness, dizziness, ataxia, headache, drowsiness, insomnia, changes in mood or mental state. Numbness or tingling in the extremities, epileptiform seizures (high doses or prolonged treatment). Transient leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Hypersensitivity reactions. Urethral discomfort and darkening of urine. Raised liver enzyme values, cholestatic hepatitis, jaundice. Thrombophlebitis (IV). Potentially Fatal: Anaphylaxis.
drugs.contraindications: History of hypersensitivity to metronidazole or other nitroimidazole derivatives. Pregnancy (1st trimester) and lactation.
drugs.interactions: Acute psychoses or confusion with disulfiram. Additive/synergistic effect with other antimicrobials. Effects reduced with phenobarbital or phenytoin. Potentially Fatal: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. Increased risk of adverse effects of coumarin anticoagulants, phenytoin, lithium, ciclosporin, fluorouracil. Increased risk of neurological effects with cimetidine.
drugs.precautions: Caution in patient with active disease of CNS except for brain abscess of hepatic encephalopathy
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2018

  • Metronidazole and tinidazole are bactericidal against anaerobes and protozoa and have a similar spectrum; there is some cross-resistance between the two.
  • This medicine may make you feel dizzy or confused; avoid driving if you are affected like this.
  • Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 24 hours after finishing the course to prevent nausea, vomiting, flushing, headache and palpitations (sometimes occur when alcohol is taken with metronidazole).
  • Stop taking metronidazole and check with your doctor immediately if you have any numbness, tingling, pain or weakness in hands or feet.
  • High-dose and/or prolonged treatment: Leukopenia is reversible and usually only occurs after prolonged treatment; peripheral neuropathy (usually reversible) and/or CNS toxicity (e.g. seizures, encephalopathy, cerebellar toxicity) are more likely.

Product leaflet, accessed 2024

  • Treatment of candidal vulvovaginitis due to Candida albicans, in bacterial vaginosis due to anerobic bacteria and Gardnerella vaginalis, in trichomonal vaginitis due to Trichomonas vaginalis and in mixed vaginal infections.

    • Dosages based on retrospective/observational data and clinical experience. Metyrapone may be administered as monotherapy or occasionally in combination with other agents (e.g. ketoconazole and/or mitotane); refer to protocols for details.

drugs.indications:
i) Treatment of invasive candidiasis, including candidemia in adults when intolerance or resistance to Amphotericin B or Fluconazole.
ii) Treatment of invasive candidiasis in children.
drugs.dosages:
i) Dosage for adults, adolescents ≥16 years of age and the elderly for the treatment of invasive candidiasis:
- Body weight >40 kg, 100 mg/day*
- Body weight ≤40 kg, 2 mg/kg/day*
*If patient's response is inadequate, e.g. persistence of cultures or if clinical condition does not improve, the dose may be increased to 200 mg/day in patients weighing >40 kg or 4 mg/kg/day in patients weighing ≤40 kg.
Treatment duration for invasive candidiasis: should be a minimum of 14 days. The antifungal treatment should continue for at least one week after two sequential negative blood cultures have been obtained and after resolution of clinical signs and symptoms of infection.

ii) Dosage for children:
- Body weight ≤40 kg, 2 mg/kg/day;
- Body weight >40 kg, 100 mg/day
drugs.adverseReactions: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, pyrexia, mucosal inflammation, rigors, peripheral edema, fatigue, hypokalemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcemia, anorexia, hyperglycemia, fluid overload, bacteremia, sepsis, cough, dyspnea, epitaxis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anemia, febrile neutropenia, rash, pruritus, headache, insomnia, anxiety, hypotension, hypertension, phlebitis, back pain, tachycardia.
drugs.contraindications: Micafungin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to any component of this medication or to other echinocandins.
drugs.interactions: Micafungin has a low potential for interactions with medicines metabolized via CYP3A mediated pathway. However, patients receiving sirolimus, nifedipine or itraconazole in combination with micafungin should be monitored for toxicity and the dosage of sirolimus, nifedipine or itraconazole should be reduced if necessary.
drugs.precautions:
- Hypersensitivity: Anaphylactic / anaphylactoid reactions including shock may occur.
- Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorder: Exfoliative cutaneous reactions, such as Steven-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrosis have been reported.
- Hemolysis: Isolated cases of hemolysis including acute intravascular hemolysis or hemolytic anemia have been reported.
- Hepatic effects: Early discontinuation in the presence of significant and persistent elevation of ALT/AST is recommended. Micafungin treatment should be conducted on a careful risk/benefit basis, particularly in patients having severe liver function impairment or chronic liver diseases.
Use in pregnancy: There are no adequate or well-controlled studies of micafungin in pregnant women.
- Use in lactation: Caution should be exercised when micafungin is administered during breastfeeding.
- Use in the elderly: No dose adjustment is necessary for the elderly.
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • The echinocandin antifungals include anidulafungin, caspofungin and micafungin. They are only active against Aspergillus spp. and Candida spp.; however, anidulafungin and micafungin are not used for the treatment of aspergillosis. Echinocandins are not effective against fungal infections of the CNS.

drugs.notes:
Product leaflet, accessed 2021

  • Toxic and inflammatory liver disorders; adjuvant in chronic liver disorders.
    • Usual dosage, 3 x 1 capsule per day after meals. For follow-up treatment, the dose can be reduced to 1-2 capsules per day.
    • There is no experience in the treatment of children. Therefore, Simepar should not be taken by children.

The Review of Natural Products, 2020

  • Milk thistle has been investigated for its anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and CNS effects. It has been studied for use in allergic rhinitis, asthma, cancer treatment-related adverse effects, rheumatoid arthritis, type 2 diabetes, drug-induced hepatotoxicity, drug-induced nephrotoxicity, dyslipidemia, and thalassemia; however clinical trials supporting these uses are limited. Milk thistle is most commonly evaluated for use in the management of liver diseases (alcohol-induced and viral hepatitis) but the majority of clinical trials show equivocal results.
  • Milk thistle is considered safe in dosages of 420 mg/day orally in divided doses for up to 41 months. One source suggests daily doses of 12 to 15 g of dry fruits for dyspepsia and disorders of the biliary system, while an extract containing 200 to 400 mg/day of silymarin is considered effective in various liver disorders.

  • Tetracyclines can discolour teeth and may cause enamel dysplasia (which increases the risk of dental caries) in children <8 years.   • Take with food or milk to reduce stomach upset.
  • Take with a large glass of water, and remain upright (do not lie down) for an hour after taking a tetracycline. This is to stop tablets or capsules sticking on the way to your stomach, and causing painful damage to the lining of your throat.
  • Do not take antacids, iron, calcium or zinc supplements within 2 hours of a tetracycline as they may interfere with its absorption.
  • Avoid sun exposure, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen while taking this medicine.
  • This medicine may cause dizziness; be careful driving or using machinery until you know how minocycline affects you. It may also cause changes in the colour of your skin or other areas: tell your doctor if this happens to you.
  • Consider limiting minocycline course to <6 months to avoid pigmentation associated with long courses; stop minocycline if pigmentation occurs.

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Microbiologically, there is little to choose between the various tetracyclines, the only exception being minocycline which has a broader spectrum; it is active against Neisseria meningitidis and has been used for meningococcal prophylaxis but is no longer recommended because of side-effects including dizziness and vertigo. Compared to other tetracyclines, minocycline is associated with a greater risk of lupus-erythematosus-like syndrome. Minocycline sometimes causes irreversible pigmentation.

drugs.brandName: Regaine for Women Regular Strength 2% Solution, Minox (Regular Strength)
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Topical application of minoxidil may stimulate limited hair growth in a small proportion of adults but only for as long as it is used.
  • Androgenetic alopecia
    • Adult, apply 1 ml twice daily, to be applied to the affected areas of scalp; discontinue if no improvement after 1 year.
  • Ensure hair and scalp dry before application.
  • Patients and their carers should be advised to wash hands after application of liquid or foam.
  • When used topically, systemic effects unlikely; only about 1-2% absorbed (greater absorption may occur with use on inflamed skin).

Rang and Dale's Pharmacology, 2020

  • Minoxidil is a vasodilator drug that was originally developed for treating hypertension. Applied topically, it is converted in hair follicles to a more potent metabolite, minoxidil sulfate (some preparations contain this salt). Perhaps because of its ability to increase blood supply to hair follicles, it stimulates growth of new hair and the progression of the new follicle through successive phases of the cell cycle. Existing follicles, usually stalled in their resting (telogen) phase, must first be 'shed' to make way for new, rapidly growing follicles, so initial hair loss following treatment is a frequent, unwelcome - and rather alarming - action of the drug. Other unwanted effects are few but some local irritation may occur. Hair loss recurs when topical application is discontinued.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Mirabegron, beta3-adrenoreceptor agonist, has similar efficacy to anticholinergics; it may be an option in people with urge incontinence who cannot tolerate anticholinergic adverse effects or when anticholinergics are not effective or contraindicated.
  • Urinary urge incontinence
    • Adult, initially 25 mg once daily; if required and tolerated, increase to 50 mg once daily.
    • Maximum 25 mg daily in people with:
      • moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class B)
      • eGFR 15-29 ml/minute/1.73 m2
      • mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh class A) or eGFR 30-89 ml/minute/1.73 m2 who are also taking strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
  • Swallow tablet whole; do not crush or chew.
  • Although mirabegron may be taken with or without food, absorption is greater if taken on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after eating).
  • It may take up to 8 weeks for full effect of 25 mg dose.
  • Monitor BP at baseline and periodically, especially in pre-existing hypertension.
  • In clinical trials, mirabegron reduced the number of incontinence episodes by about 0.8 in 48 hours compared to placebo (similar to anticholinergics).
  • Long-term safety and efficacy data are lacking (the key trials lasted 12 weeks).

Lexidrug, 2026

  • Angioedema of the face, lips, tongue and/or larynx has been reported with use of mirabegron.
  • Dose-related cardiovascular effects have been described with use of mirabegron, including hypertension, tachycardia and palpitations.
  • Use of mirabegron may result in urinary retention, especially in patients with bladder outlet obstruction, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and with/or with use of concomitant muscarinic antagonists (e.g. solifenacin, tolterodine).

drugs.indications: Symptomatic treatment of urgency, increased micturition frequency and/or urgency incontinence as may occur in adult patients with overactive bladder (OAB) syndrome.
drugs.prescribingRestrictions: For patients who are not responsive, intolerant or unsuitable to use other existing agents.
drugs.dosages: 50 mg once daily. Should be taken once daily, with liquid, swallowed whole and is not to be chewed, divided, or crushed.
drugs.adverseReactions: Tachycardia, urinary tract infections, nausea, constipation, diarrhea, headache and dizziness
drugs.contraindications:
- Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section lists of excipients.
- Severe uncontrolled hypertension defined as systolic blood pressure ≥180 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥110 mmHg
drugs.interactions: Ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, clarithromycin, metoprolol, thioridazine, type 1C antiarrhythmics (e.g. flecainide, propafenone), tricyclic antidepressants (e.g. imipramine, desipramine), digoxin and dabigatran.
drugs.precautions: Renal impairment, hepatic impairment, increases in blood pressure, patients with congenital or acquired QT prolongation, patients with bladder outlet obstruction and patients taking antimuscarinics medications for OAB.

drugs.indications: Major depression
drugs.prescribingRestrictions: Consultant/specialists for specific indications only, including Geriatricians and Neurologists
drugs.dosages: Initially 15 mg daily at bedtime increased according to response up to 45 mg daily as a single dose at bedtime or in 2 divided doses. Child and adolescent under 18 years, not recommended
drugs.adverseReactions: Agranulocytopenia, neutropenia, mania, dizziness, increase appetite & weight, GI disturbance, hypotension, somnolence. Patients should be advised to report any fever, sore throat, stomatitis or other signs of infection during treatment. Blood count should be performed and the drug to be stopped immediately if blood dyscrasia suspected, raised serum cholesterol and serum triglycerides, raised ALT (SGPT) level, asthenia, dizziness, dream disorder, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, seizure, worsening depression, suicidal ideation, dry mouth. NPRA Safety Alert (20 Apr 2021): i) Amnesia ii) Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS).
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to mirtazapine or component of formulation, MAOIs, procarbazine, selegiline
drugs.interactions: Clonidine, monoamine oxidase inhibitors, ethanol, warfarin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, ketoconazole, cimetidine, methadone, rifampicin, antivirals, St. John's wort, diazepam, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, linezolid, olanzapine, tramadol, venlafaxine
drugs.precautions: Heart disease, hypotension, epilepsy, diabetes, hepatic and renal impairment, pregnancy, mania and hypomania, hyponatremia, bone marrow depression (granulocytopenia), jaundice, hypersensitivity to other anti-depressant, suicidal ideation and behavior or worsening depression; increased risk in children and adolescents.
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2023

  • Major depressive disorder (unipolar)
    • Adult, initial: 15 mg once daily at bedtime; increase dose in 15 mg increments at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability. Maximum dose: 45 mg/day (manufacturer's labeling); however, doses up to 60 mg/day have been used in clinical trials.
  • Headache, chronic tension-type prophylaxis (alternative agent) (off-label use)
    • Adult, initial: 15 mg once daily at bedtime; may increase after 1 week to 30 mg/day based on response and tolerability.
  • Administer without regard to meals.
  • Orally disintegrating tablet: Do not remove tablet from blister pack until ready to administer; peel back foil to expose tablet; use dry hands to remove tablet and place immediately on tongue. Tablet dissolves rapidly in saliva; water is not needed. Do not chew, crush or split tablet.
  • Sedation (drowsiness) is very common with initial use and may cause nonadherence, dizziness and confusion, particularly in older adults. However, the dose relationship with mirtazapine is unique, in that lower doses (≤15 mg) are associated with significant sedation compared to less sedation with higher doses (>15 mg). Tolerance appears to develop to the sedative effect.

British National Formulary 85, 2023

  • Patient should be advised to report any fever, sore throat, stomatitis or other signs of infection during treatment. Blood count should be performed and the drug stopped immediately if blood dyscrasia suspected.
  • Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, agitation, anxiety and headache are most common features of withdrawal if treatment stopped abruptly or if dose reduced markedly, dose should be reduced over several weeks.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine may cause drowsiness and may increase the effects of alcohol; do not drive or operate machinery if you are affected. Sedative action may be useful for depression where insomnia is a feature
  • Increased suicidal thoughts and behavior can occur soon after starting antidepressants, particularly in young people; monitor patients frequently and carefully early in treatment.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2021

  • Although mirtazapine is better tolerated than the TCAs, it still has a pronounced sedative effect, together with increased appetite, weight gain, constipation, and asthenia. Abnormal liver function tests may occur, and there appears to be a very small risk of neutropenia or agranulocytosis. Lower doses may be sedating, whereas higher doses may cause insomnia.

drugs.genericName: Mirvetuximab Soravtansine 5 mg/ml Concentrate for Solution for Infusion
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 92, 2026

  • Ovarian cancer; Fallopian tube cancer; Peritoneal cancer
    • Adult, by intravenous infusion, access specialist resources for dosing information.
  • Females of childbearing potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for 7 months after last treatment.

Lexidrug, 2026

  • Mirvetuximab soravtansine can cause severe ocular toxicities, including visual impairment, keratopathy, dry eye, photophobia, eye pain, and uveitis. Conduct an ophthalmic exam, including visual acuity and slit lamp exam, prior to initiation of mirvetuximab soravtansine, every other cycle for the first 8 cycles, and as clinically indicated. Administer prophylactic artificial tears and ophthalmic topical steroids. Withhold mirvetuximab soravtansine for ocular toxicities until improvement and resume at the same or reduced dose. Discontinue mirvetuximab soravtansine for grade 4 ocular toxicities.
  • Store intact vials at 2-8°C; do not freeze. Store vials upright. Store in original carton to protect from light. Do not shake.

drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2024

  • NSAID-induced gastric ulcers, prevention
    • Adult, 200 mcg 4 times daily; if not tolerated, may decrease dose to 100 mcg 4 times daily.
  • Incomplete abortion, treatment (off-label use)
    • Adult, 600 mcg as a single dose in patients <14 weeks' gestation.
    • A systematic review suggests additional data may be needed to determine the most effective dose and route of administration.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Termination up to 63 days gestation
    • Give 36-48 hours after mifepristone.
    • Do not use oral route after 49 days gestation as it is less effective than buccal route.
    • Oral, buccal, 800 micrograms as a single dose (or in 2 doses of 400 micrograms 2 hours apart). A repeat dose may be appropriate.
  • Take with meals to reduce the risk of diarrhoea.
  • Tell your doctor if you have symptoms such as black stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.

Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics, 2019

  • Treatment for ulcer prophylaxis is now considered cost-effective for all patients who require NSAIDs for any period of time, not just in those at high risk. Options include cotherapy with acid-suppressing agents or a synthetic prostaglandin analogue, or substitution of a selective COX-2 inhibitor for a nonselective NSAID.
  • The prostaglandin analogue misoprostol at a dose of 800 micrograms daily has the strongest evidence of being effective at reducing NSAID-associated ulcer complications and symptomatic ulcers. However, it is rarely used in practice because adverse effects, primarily diarrhoea, abdominal pain and nausea, limit its use, and lower doses are less effective.

drugs.indications:
i) Gastrointestinal, lung, breast, cervical cancers
ii) Bladder tumors
iii) Ophthalmological conditions: conjunctival squamous neoplasia, squamous cell carcinoma of conjunctiva, trabeculectomy chronic lymphocytic leukemia, chronic myelogenous leukemia. Gastric, colorectal, lung cancer
drugs.dosages:
i) 10-20 mg/m2 body surface area (BSA) given as a single dose through a running IV infusion repeated every 6-8 weeks. The whole schedule may be repeated depending on the bone marrow
ii) 10-40 mg daily or every other day (intravesical)
iii) 0.4 mg topically as a single application for ophthalmological conditions, duration: 1 to 3 minutes
drugs.adverseReactions: Nephrotoxicity, delayed myelosuppression, nausea and vomiting, alopecia, congestive heart failure, fever, hemolytic uremic syndrome-risk increase when cumulative dose more than 50 mg/m2, interstitial pneumonitis
drugs.contraindications: Thrombocytopenia, coagulation disorders, pregnancy, lactation, hypersensitivity to mitomycin, hepatotoxicity
drugs.interactions: Vinblastine, vince alkaloids may increase risk of cardiotoxicity when given together with mitomycin C
drugs.precautions: Bleeding tendency, radiotherapy, extravasation, hepatic dysfunction, myelosuppression, renal impairment
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Tell your doctor or nurse immediately if you feel any pain, stinging or burning during the injection or infusion.
  • Myelosuppression may develop up to 8 weeks after a dose; it is cumulative. Thrombocytopenia usually occurs within 2-4 weeks after initial dose; temporary recovery may occur, followed by nadir at 4-6 weeks. Neutropenia usually occurs within 2-4 weeks, with nadir at 6 weeks. Anaemia occurs less frequently.
  • Pulmonary toxicity
    • Usually presents as dyspnoea with non-productive cough and pulmonary infiltrates. Stop mitomycin; corticosteroids have been tried (efficacy unclear).
    • There are reports of acute shortness of breath and severe bronchospasm occurring minutes to hours after administration of a vinca alkaloid in patients who have received mitomycin.
    • Pulmonary hypertension has also been rarely reported.

drugs.indications: Acute leukemia, elderly patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), relapsed/resistant acute leukemia, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL)
drugs.dosages:
10-12 mg/m2 IV daily for 3 days, in combination with other cytotoxic agents. Refer to protocol. Child, 5-10 mg/m2 daily for 3-5 days according to protocol.
Treatment of acute leukemia: Adult, 8-12 mg/m2/day once daily for 4-5 days. Child more than 2 years, same as adult dose. Child 2 years, 0.4 mg/kg/day once daily for 3-5 days
drugs.adverseReactions: Myelosuppression, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, alopecia, hepatotoxicity, congestive cardiac failure, constipation, diarrhea, arrhythmias, discoloration of urine and other secretions, alopecia, secondary malignancy, fatigue, fever, headache, amenorrhea, abdominal pain, acute myeloid leukemia, myelodysplasia of the spinal cord
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to mitoxantrone products, pregnancy, lactation, severe myelosuppression, cardiac dysfunction
drugs.interactions: Increased risk of infection by the live vaccine, trastuzumab
drugs.precautions: Myelosuppression or poor general condition in cases with functional cardiac changes including congestive heart failure and decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction, hepatic insufficiency, children, pregnancy, lactation
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Give by slow IV injection or short infusion into side-arm of a fast-running infusion. Avoid extravasation. Venous sclerosis may occur if the same vein is used for repeated cycles.
  • Urine and possibly whites of eyes may appear blue-green for 1-2 days after dose.
  • Myelosuppression is common, affecting white cells, and to a lesser degree, platelets and red cells. The white cell count nadir occurs about 10 days after a dose, with recovery by about 21 days.

British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Manufacturer advises effective contraception during and for at least 6 months after treatment in men or women.

British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Neuromuscular blockade (short duration) during surgery and intubation
    • Adult, initially by intravenous injection, 70-250 micrograms/kg; (by intravenous injection) maintenance 100 micrograms/kg every 15 minutes, alternatively (by intravenous infusion) maintenance 8-10 micrograms/kg/minute, (by intravenous infusion) adjusted in steps of 1 microgram/kg/minute every 3 minutes if required; (by intravenous infusion) usual dose 6-7 micrograms/kg/minute.
  • To avoid excessive dosage in obese patients, dose should be calculated on the basis of ideal body-weight.

MIMS, 2022

  • Store at 2°C to 8°C. Protect from light. Do not freeze.

drugs.contraindications: Acute confusional state, hypersensitivity to moclobemide, concomitant use with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, conventional MAOIs or tricyclic antidepressants, concomitant use of narcotics
drugs.interactions: Tricyclic antidepressants, beta-2 agonist, carbamazepine
drugs.precautions: Avoid in excited and agitated patient, thyrotoxicosis, hepatic impairment, pregnancy, lactation, hypertensive, avoid ingestion of excessive amounts of tyramine-rich foods, occipital headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, tachycardia or bradycardia, coadministration with dextromethorphan resulted in vertigo, tremor, nausea and vomiting
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Moclobemide is best taken with, or soon after, food.
  • Take doses no later than early afternoon or you may have trouble sleeping at night.
  • Although moclobemide is unlikely to affect your ability to drive or operate machinery, be careful with these types of tasks until you know how you are affected.
  • Avoid use in acute confusional states
  • Increased suicidal thoughts and behaviour can occur soon after starting antidepressants, particularly in young people; monitor patients frequently and carefully early in treatment.
  • Low tyramine diet is not usually required below the maximum dose.
  • Relatively nontoxic in overdose, and less likely to cause sexual dysfunction than nonselective MAOIs and SSRIs
  • Moclobemide, a reversible, selective MAOI, has far less potential for interactions than the nonselective MAOIs and is safe for most people if used within recommended dose range. It is relatively safe in overdose.

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Moclobemide is claimed to cause less potentiation of the pressor effect of tyramine than the traditional (irreversible) MAOIs, but patients should avoid consuming large amounts of tyramine-rich food (such as mature cheese, yeast extracts and fermented soya bean products).
  • Withdrawal effects may occur within 5 days of stopping treatment with antidepressant drugs; they are usually mild and self-limiting, but in some cases may be severe. The risk of withdrawal symptoms is increased if the antidepressant is stopped suddenly after regular administration for 8 weeks or more. The dose should preferably be reduced gradually over about 4 weeks, or longer if withdrawal symptoms emerge (6 months in patients who have been on long-term maintenance treatment).

drugs.indications: For primary volume replacement in hypovolemia, peri-operative stabilization of the circulation, hemodilution, extracorporeal circulation (hemodialysis and heart-lung machine)
drugs.dosages: Adult, 500-1500 ml given as IV infusion
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypersensitivity reactions, severe anaphylactoid
drugs.contraindications: Not known
drugs.interactions: Not known
drugs.precautions: Patients with cardiac disease. NPRA Safety Alert (26 Oct 2018): Risk of sensitization and consequent anaphylactic reaction to gelatin-containing solutions could be highly increased in patients with history of allergy to red meat (mammal meat) and offal, and/or those who tested positive for anti-alpha-gal IgE antibodies.
drugs.notes:
Australian Injectable Drugs Handbook, 2020

  • Infusion reactions including urticaria and flushing to severe reactions e.g. anaphylaxis, hypotension, shock, bronchospasm, cardiac or respiratory arrest may occur in both conscious and anaesthetised patients.
  • Monitor the patient for signs of anaphylaxis and of circulatory overload e.g. dyspnoea and jugular vein congestion. Stop the infusion immediately if symptoms appear and treat accordingly.
  • Blood may be given through the same giving set as Gelofusine. Gelofusine has negligible calcium content and will not clot citrated blood.
  • Gelofusine may be used to reconstitute packed red cells.
  • Contains gelatin derived from bovine source.

drugs.brandName: Elomet, Bitvio, Elolo, Elosone, Momate, Melomet, Metasone, Vizomet
drugs.indications: For the relief of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid responsive dermatoses
drugs.dosages: Apply thin layer to the affected skin areas once daily until the lesion heals or for a duration of 3 weeks whichever is sooner. Massage gently and thoroughly until the medication disappears.
drugs.adverseReactions: Burning, folliculitis, acneiform reaction, pruritus, paresthesia, tingling or stinging, and signs of skin atrophy.
drugs.contraindications: Patients who are sensitive to mometasone furoate, to other corticosteroids or to any component of the product.
drugs.interactions: CYP3A4
drugs.precautions: Systemic absorption may be increased if extensive body surface are treated. Do not use occlusive dressing. Long term use in infant and children. Avoid contact with eyes, pregnancy, lactation
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Severe inflammatory skin disorders such as eczemas unresponsive to less potent corticosteroids; Psoriasis
    • Child 2-17 years, apply once daily, to be applied thinly (to scalp in case of lotion).
    • Adult, apply once daily, to be applied thinly (to scalp in case of lotion)
  • Topical corticosteroids should be applied in sufficient quantity to cover the affected areas.
  • The length of cream or ointment expelled from a tube may be used to specify the quantity to be applied to a given area of skin. This length can be measured in terms of a fingertip unit (the distance from the tip of the adult index finger to the first crease). One fingertip unit (approximately 500 mg from a tube with a standard 5 mm diameter nozzle) is sufficient to cover an area that is twice that of the flat adult handprint (palm and fingers).
  • Several minutes should elapse between application of different preparations.
  • Potency at 0.01%: potent
  • Patients and their carers should be reassured that side effects such as skin thinning and systemic effects rarely occur when topical corticosteroids are used appropriately.
