  • Manufacturer recommends refrigeration of intact vials at 2-8°C and may be stored at room temperature for 14 days; however, additional testing has demonstrated stability for ≤6 months unrefrigerated (25°C).

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Suxamethonium mimics acetylcholine; acts at acetylcholine receptor, depolarising the motor end plate resulting in neuromuscular blockade.
  • You may have muscle pains for about 24 hours after your operation, particularly around your neck, shoulders and chest.
  • Useful for procedures in which a rapid onset and short duration of action is required.
  • After IV administration, the onset of action occurs in 30-60 seconds and lasts for 3-5 minutes; after IM injection (rarely indicated), onset usually occurs in 3 minutes and lasts 10-30 minutes; larger doses produce more prolonged muscle relaxation.

drugs.indications: Diagnostic test to differentiate primary adrenal from secondary (pituitary) adrenocortical insufficiency
drugs.dosages: Diagnostic test for investigation of adrenocortical insufficiency. Adult, as plain preparation: Measure plasma cortisol concentration immediately before and exactly 30 min after IM/IV inj of 250 mcg. Post-inj rise in plasma cortisol concentration ≥200 nmol/l (70 mcg/l) if normal adrenocortical function. As depot preparation (if inconclusive results with plain preparation): Measure plasma cortisol concentration before and exactly 30 min, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 hr after an IM inj of 1 mg tetracosactide acetate depot. Adrenocortical function normal if the post-inj rise in plasma cortisol concentration increases 2-fold in 1st hr, and continues to rise steadily. Expected levels in 1st hr: 600-1,250 nmol/l, increasing slowly up to 1000-1800 nmol/l by 5th hr. Child, IV 250 mcg/1.73 m2 BSA. Intramuscular.
drugs.adverseReactions: Bradycardia, hypertension, peripheral edema, tachycardia, rash, whealing with redness at the injection site, anaphylaxis, hypersensitivity reaction
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled acute infections, active or quiescent TB. Live vaccines. History of allergic disorders e.g. asthma. Pregnancy and lactation (therapeutic use).
drugs.interactions: Decreased effect: Spironolactone, hydrocortisone, cortisone
drugs.precautions: Due to side effects or potentially fatal allergic reactions, therefore, patients should be monitored for at least one hour after administration in a controlled setting. Discontinue treatment by reducing the dosage gradually
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Tetracosactide (tetracosactrin), an analogue of corticotropin (ACTH), is used to test adrenocortical function; failure of the plasma cortisol concentration to rise after administration of tetracosactide indicates adrenocortical insufficiency.
  • Both corticotropin and tetracosactide were formerly used as alternatives to corticosteroids in conditions such as Crohn's disease or rheumatoid arthritis; their value was limited by the variable and unpredictable therapeutic response and by the waning of their effect with time.

Product leaflet, accessed 2022

  • Store at 2-8°C.
  • Store in the original packaging to protect the product from light.

drugs.indications: For short-term and intermittent long-term therapy in the treatment of patients with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in whom the use of alternative, conventional therapies are deemed inadvisable because of potential risks, or in the treatment of patients who are not adequately responsive to or are intolerant of alternative, conventional therapies
drugs.dosages:
Adult ≥16 years, apply 0.03% or 0.1% to the affected skin twice daily and rub in gently and completely. Children ≥2 years, apply 0.03% ointment thinly to the affected skin BD and rub in gently and completely.

Treatment should be continued for 1 week after clearing of signs & symptoms of atopic dermatitis.
drugs.adverseReactions: Skin burning, pruritus, skin erythema, skin tingling, folliculitis, acne, herpes simplex. Increased skin sensitivity, alcohol intolerance.
drugs.contraindications: Patients with a history of hypersensitivity to tacrolimus or any other component of product. Congenital epidermal barrier defects; generalized erythroderma; immunodeficiency; concomitant use with drugs that cause immunosuppression (may be prescribed in exceptional circumstances by specialists); application to malignant or potentially malignant skin lesions; avoid contact with eyes and mucous membranes; application under occlusion; breast-feeding
drugs.interactions: The concomitant administration of known CYP3A4 inhibitors in patients with widespread and/or erythrodermic disease should be done with caution. Some examples of such drugs are erythromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, fluconazole, calcium-channel blockers and cimetidine.
drugs.precautions: Minimize exposure to sunlight or UV light, therapy with UVB or UVA in combination with psoralens should be avoided. Clinical infections at treatment sites should be resolved before treatment. Avoid use with occlusive dressings & contact with mucous membranes. Hepatic failure, generalized erythroderma. Use in patients with genetic epidermal barrier defects (e.g. Netherton's syndrome) is not recommended. Avoid in pregnancy. Lactation.
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2023

  • Atopic dermatitis (moderate to severe)
    • Treatment: Apply thin layer of 0.03% or 0.1% ointment to affected area twice daily; rub in gently and completely. Discontinue use when symptoms have cleared. If no improvement within 6 weeks, patients should be re-examined to confirm diagnosis.
    • Maintenance therapy (off-label use): Apply one application (thin layer of 0.03% or 0.1% ointment) to areas usually affected twice daily twice a week.
  • Psoriasis (intertriginous and facial) (off-label use)
    • Adult, apply thin layer of 0.1% ointment to affected area twice daily; the treatment period in clinical trials was 6 to 8 weeks.
  • Vitiligo (primarily the head and neck region) (off-label use)
    • Adult, apply thin layer of 0.1% ointment to affected area twice daily; reassess every 3 to 6 months for adequate response.
  • Tacrolimus ointment is not indicated for use in children younger than 2 years of age. Only tacrolimus 0.03% ointment is indicated for use in children 2 to 15 years of age.
  • Although a causal relationship has not been established, rare cases of malignancy (i.e., skin cancer and lymphoma) have been reported in patients treated with topical calcineurin inhibitors, including tacrolimus ointment. Avoid continuous long-term use of topical calcineurin inhibitors, including tacrolimus ointment, in any age group, and limit application to areas of involvement with atopic dermatitis.

  • Generally, improvement is seen within one week of starting treatment. If no signs of improvement are seen after two weeks of treatment, further treatment options should be considered.
  • Protopic ointment may be used on any part of the body, including face, neck and flexure areas, except on mucous membranes.
  • Protopic ointment should not be applied under occlusion because this method of administration has not been studied in patients.
  • Exposure of the skin to sunlight should be minimized and the use of UV light from a solarium, therapy with UVB or UVA in combination with psoralens should be avoided during use of Protopic ointment.

drugs.indications:
i) Primary immunosuppression in liver and kidney allograft recipients, and liver and kidney allograft rejection resistant to conventional immunosuppressive agents. It is recommended to be used concomitantly with adrenal corticosteroids. Because of the risk of anaphylaxis, injection should be reserved for patients unable to take capsules only.
ii) Class III/IV/V Lupus nephritis (in a case where the effect of steroids is insufficient or administration of steroids is difficult because of their adverse reactions).
drugs.dosages:
i) 0.1-0.2 mg/kg/day for liver transplantation and at 0.15-0.3 mg/kg/day for kidney transplantation administered as 2 divided doses.
ii) 3 mg once daily (to be administered as 2 divided doses).

Dosing is individualised and according to product insert/protocol.
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypertension, angina, tachycardia, pleural and pericardial effusion, hypotension, arrhythmias, ventricular or septal hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, gastrointestinal disturbances, headache, tremor, dizziness, anxiety, confusion and infection
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to tacrolimus products, macrolides, polyoxyethylated castor oil (parenteral formulation) or structurally related compounds, pregnancy and lactation
drugs.interactions: Aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, additive or synergistic renal function impairment. Spironolactone, hyperkalemia. NSAIDs, acute renal failure. Live vaccines, risk of infection in immunocompromised hosts, reduced effectiveness of vaccine. Fluconazole, nifedipine, diltiazem, clarithromycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, increased risk of tacrolimus toxicity (nephrotoxicity, hyperglycemia, hyperkalemia)
drugs.precautions: Renal or hepatic insufficiency, monitor blood glucose levels, increased risk of infections and possibly lymphoma, hyperkalemia, hypertension, myocardial hypertrophy and neurotoxicity. Monitor blood pressure, ECG, visual status, electrolytes (especially K), hematology parameters. Children less than 2 year who are Epstein-Barr virus sero-negative. Patients with allergenic disposition. May impair ability to drive or operate machinery. Continuous IV therapy should not be continued for more than 7 days. Avoid excessive exposure to sun or UV light. Increased risk for opportunistic infections such as activation of latent viral infections including BK virus -associated nephropathy.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Calcineurin inhibitors: Diarrhoea, tremor, hyperglycaemia and diabetes are more common with tacrolimus; hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hirsutism and gingival hyperplasia are more common with ciclosporin.
  • Take capsules at the same time each day and in the same way (always with food or always on an empty stomach).
    • Although tacrolimus is best absorbed on an empty stomach, compliance may be improved if it is taken with a meal; emphasise the importance of taking it consistently with regard to food
  • Grapefruit juice and many other drugs interact with this medicine; avoid grapefruit juice and tell your doctor and pharmacist that you are taking this medicine before starting any new medicines.
  • Avoid sun exposure, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen.
  • Acute nephrotoxicity is dose-related and reversible with dose reduction or withdrawal. Chronic nephrotoxicity occurs with long-term use, is unrelated to dosage, potentially irreversible and involves permanent renal structural changes (e.g. interstitial fibrosis).
  • Neurotoxicity: Tremor and headache are most frequent; other effects include paraesthesia, confusion, seizures, coma, psychosis. Reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy syndrome has also been reported.

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Inadvertent switching between oral tacrolimus products has been associated with reports of toxicity and graft rejection. To ensure maintenance of therapeutic response when a patient is stabilised on a particular brand, oral tacrolimus products should be prescribed and dispensed by brand name only.
    • Adoport®, Prograf®, Capexion® and Tacni® are immediate-release capsules that are taken twice daily, once in the morning and once in the evening;
    • Modigraf® granules are used to prepare an immediate-release oral suspension which is taken twice daily, once in the morning and once in the evening;
    • Advagraf® is a prolonged-release capsule that is taken once daily in the morning.
    • Switching between tacrolimus brands requires careful supervision and therapeutic monitoring by an appropriate specialist.
    • Important: Envarsus® is not interchangeable with other oral tacrolimus containing products; the MHRA has advised (June 2012) that oral tacrolimus products should be prescribed and dispensed by brand only.
  • After initial dosing, and for maintenance treatment, tacrolimus doses should be adjusted according to whole-blood concentration.
  • Monitor whole blood-tacrolimus trough concentration (especially during episodes of diarrhea).
  • Monitor blood pressure, ECG (for hypertrophic changes - risk of cardiomyopathy), fasting blood-glucose concentration, hematological and neurological (including visual) and coagulation parameters, electrolytes, hepatic and renal function.

drugs.indications:
i) Prophylaxis of transplant rejection in adult kidney or liver allograft recipients.
ii) Treatment of kidney or liver allograft rejection resistant to treatment with other immunosuppressive medicinal products in adult.
drugs.dosages:
i) Prophylaxis of transplant rejection:
a) Kidney Transplant, Tacrolimus PR therapy should commence at dose of 0.20-0.30 mg/kg/day administered once daily in the morning. Administration should commence within 24 hours after completion of surgery.
b) Liver Transplant, Tacrolimus PR therapy should commence at a dose of 0.10-0.20 mg/kg/day administered once daily in the morning. Administration should commence within 12-18 hours after completion of surgery.

ii) Treatment of allograft rejection: For conversion:
a) From other immunosuppressants to once daily Tacrolimus PR, treatment should begin with the initial oral dose recommended in kidney and liver transplantation respectively for prophylaxis of transplant rejection.
b) From Tacrolimus to Tacrolimus PR, allograft transplant patients maintained on twice daily Tacrolimus capsules dosing requiring conversion to once daily Tacrolimus PR should be converted on a 1:1 (mg:mg) total daily dose basis. Tacrolimus PR should be administered in the morning.
drugs.adverseReactions: Ischemic coronary artery disorders, tachycardia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, red blood cell analyses abnormal, leukocytosis, headache, tremor, eye disorders, vision blurred, photophobia, tinnitus, parenchymal lung disorders, dyspnea, pleural effusion, cough, pharyngitis, nasal congestion, inflammations, diarrhea, nausea, renal impairment, rash, pruritis, alopecias, acne, sweating increased, arthralgia, back pain, muscle cramps, pain in limb, diabetes mellitus, hyperglycemic conditions, hyperkalemia, hypertension, insomnia.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to tacrolimus, or any of the excipients. Hypersensitivity to other macrolides.
drugs.interactions: Monitor for tacrolimus blood level and adjust dose when substances with a potential for interaction -strong inhibitors of CYP3A4 (e.g. telaprevir, boceprevir, ritonavir, ketoconazole, voriconazole, itraconazole, telithromycin or clarithromycin) or inducers of CYP3A4 (e.g. rifampicin, rifabutin) is combined with tacrolimus. Combination of tacrolimus with drugs known to have nephrotoxic or neurotoxic effects may increase the risk of these effects. Avoid high potassium intake or potassium-sparing diuretics, live attenuated vaccines.
drugs.precautions: Patient should be maintained on a single formulation of tacrolimus with the corresponding daily dosing regimen; alteration in formulation or regimen should only take place under the close supervision of a transplant specialist. For treatment of allograft rejection resistant to treatment with other immunosuppressive medicinal products in adult patients clinical data are not yet available for the prolonged-release formulation of tacrolimus. Avoid exposure to sunlight and UV light. Increased risk for opportunistic infections (bacterial, fungal, viral and protozoal) such as BK virus-associated nephropathy and JC virus associated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Increased risk of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRS). Therapeutic drug monitoring is required.

  • Erectile dysfunction
    • Intermittent use
      • Take orally 30 minutes-12 hours before sexual activity (may be effective for up to 36 hours); no more than 1 dose daily. If required at least twice a week, consider daily use.

    • Oral, 5 mg once daily.

If a nitrate is required after a PDE5 inhibitor has been taken, wait at least 24 hours with sildenafil or vardenafil, 12 hours with avanafil and 48 hours with tadalafil before giving the nitrate. drugs.indications: Reduction of intraocular pressure (IOP) in adult patients with primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) or ocular hypertension (OHT) who are insufficiently responsive to topical monotherapy with beta-blockers or prostaglandin analogues and require a combination therapy, and who would benefit from preservative free eye drops
drugs.prescribingRestrictions:
- As third line of treatment in patients with POAG or OHT who require fixed-dose combination therapy.
- To be prescribed by Glaucoma consultants only
drugs.dosages: Instill 1 drop in the affected eye(s) once daily.
drugs.adverseReactions: Conjunctival/ocular hyperemia, eye pruritus, eye pain, change of eyelashes (increased length, thickness and number of lashes), eyelash discoloration, eye irritation, foreign body sensation in eyes, blurred vision, photophobia.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or to any of the excipients. drugs.precautions: Systemic adverse reactions, cardiac disorders (e.g. coronary heart disease, Prinzmetal's angina and cardiac failure) and hypotension, severe peripheral circulatory disturbance/disorders (e.g. severe forms of Raynaud's disease or Raynaud's syndrome), respiratory disorders (e.g. asthma, mild/moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)), hypoglycemia/diabetes, corneal diseases (dryness of the eyes), angle-closure glaucoma, history of atopy or a history of severe anaphylactic reaction, choroidal detachment, surgical anesthesia, aphakic patients, pseudophakic patients, cystoid macular oedema or iritis/uveitis, pregnant and breastfeeding women.

  • Glaucoma and ocular hypertension

  • A paradoxical increase in intraocular pressure may occur if 2 ocular prostaglandin analogues are used together; avoid combination.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Tell your doctor if you develop abnormal vaginal bleeding, vaginal discharge or pain or pressure in the pelvic region while you are taking tamoxifen or after you have stopped taking it.
  • Tamoxifen is metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to active metabolites.
  • Compared with tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors are associated with less endometrial hyperplasia and VTE but more arthralgia, myalgia, bone fractures and cardiovascular disease.

British National Formulary 86, 2023

  • Tamoxifen can increase the risk of thromboembolism particularly during and immediately after major surgery or periods of immobility (consider interrupting treatment and initiating anticoagulant measures).

drugs.dosages: 400 mcg once daily
drugs.adverseReactions: Abnormal ejaculation, reduced libido, priapism, intra-operative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS), dizziness, syncope, palpitations, postural hypotension, rhinitis, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, rash, angioedema, asthenia, drowsiness, blurred vision

drugs.interactions: Drugs which may reduce blood pressure, cimetidine, fluoxetine, ketoconazole, sildenafil
drugs.precautions: Patients receiving antihypertensive treatment, elderly patients, hepatic and renal impairment, during cataract surgery (risk of intra-operative floppy iris syndrome)
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2018

  • Swallow whole, do not crush or chew.
  • All selective alpha-blockers appear to be similarly effective for BPH. Silodosin, tamsulosin and alfuzosin have less effect on BP than prazosin or terazosin and may be a better choice for BPH. Dosage titration is required with prazosin and terazosin to minimise hypotensive effects.
  • Dizziness on standing may occur especially when starting treatment or when the dose is increased. Get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimise this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy. Take the first dose at bedtime, but be careful if you get up during the night as you may feel dizzy.
  • This medicine may cause drowsiness or dizziness; do not drive or operate machinery if affected.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2021

  • Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome is a concern with α-blockers, especially tamsulosin. Men with LUTS being offered α-blockers should be asked about planned cataract surgery. Men with planned cataract surgery should avoid starting α-blockers until their cataract surgery is completed. If already taking an α-blocker, the patient needs to inform his surgeon so that precautions can be taken.

drugs.indications: Sodium pertechnetate is used for scintigraphy or nuclear scan particularly of the brain and thyroid to prepare various technetium-99 m labelled injections for selective organ imaging
drugs.dosages:
Technetium-99 m as pertechnetate is obtained by elution with a sterile solution of Sodium Chloride 0.9%. The dosage depend on type of scan
i) Thyroid scintigraphy: 18.5-80 MBq (0.5-2.2 mCi) Scintigraphy performed 20 minutes after intravenous injection
ii) Salivary gland scintigraphy: 40 MBq (1.1 mCi) Scintigraphy performed immediately after intravenous injection and at regular intervals up to 15 minutes
iii) Meckel's diverticulum scintigraphy: 400 MBq (10.8 mCi) Scintigraphy performed immediately after intravenous injection and at regular interval up to 30 minutes
iv) Brain scintigraphy: 370-800 MBq (10-22 mCi) Rapid sequential images are taken immediately within the first minute after intravenous administration, static images 1 to 4 hours later. Thyroid and coriod plexus should be blocked to avoid non-specific 99 mTc uptake
v) Cardiac and vascular scintigraphy: 740-925 MBq (20-25 mCi) Red cells are labelled in vivo or in vitro by pre-treating with a reducing agent. Dynamic images are taken in the first minute after intravenous administration, followed by regular images over 30 minutes
vi) Gastrointestinal bleeding: 740-925 MBq (20-25 mCi) Red cells are labelled in vivo or in vitro by pre-treating with a reducing agent. Dynamic images are taken in the first minutes after intravenous administration, followed by regular images at appropriate intervals for up to 24 hours
vii) Lacrimal duct scintigraphy: 2-4 MBq each eye (50-100 mCi) Drops are instilled into eye and dynamic images are taken over 2 minutes, followed by static images at appropriate intervals over 20 minutes
drugs.adverseReactions: Allergic reactions include urticaria, facial edema, vasodilation, pruritus, cardiac arrythmias and coma. Exposure to ionizing radiation is linked with cancer induction and a potential for development of hereditary defects. For diagnostic nuclear medicine investigation, the current evidence suggest that these adverse effects will occur with low frequency because of low radiation doses incurred
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy and lactation
drugs.interactions: Drug interaction have been reported in brain scintigraphy where there can be increased uptake of pertechnetate in the walls of cerebral ventricles as a result of methotrexate induced ventriculitis. In abdominal imaging, drugs such as atropine, isoprenaline and analgesics can result in a delay in gastric emptying and redistribution of pertechnetate
drugs.precautions: Radiopharmaceuticals may be received, used and administered only by authorized persons in designated clinical setting with appropriate government authorization for the use and manipulation of radionuclides. Their receipt, storage, use, transfer and disposal are subject to the regulations and or appropriate licenses of the local competent official organizations. After use, materials associated with the preparation and administration of radiopharmaceuticals including any unused product and its container, should be decontaminated or treated as radioactive waste and disposed of in accordance with the conditions specified by the local competent authority. The administration of radiopharmaceuticals creates risk for other persons from external radiation or contamination from spills of urine, vomiting etc. Radiation protection precautions in accordance with national regulations must therefore be taken

  • You may feel dizzy when you start taking this medicine. Get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimize this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy or light-headed.

    • stop potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics

drugs.indications:
In patients with glioblastoma multiforme who fulfil all the following criteria:
i. Total /near total resection
ii. ECOG/WHO performance status 0-2
iii. Age less than 60 years
drugs.dosages: Concomitant phase: 75 mg/m2 daily with radiotherapy for 42 days, followed by 6 cycle of adjuvant treatment. Adjuvant phase: Additional 6 cycles of adjuvant phase. Cycle 1, 150 mg/m2 once daily for 5 days followed by 23 days without treatment. Cycle 2-6, 200 mg/m2 once daily for 5 days per 28-day cycle
drugs.adverseReactions: GI disturbances, anorexia, headache, fatigue, alopecia, rash, blurred vision, hearing impairment, dizziness, fever, muscle weakness.
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, lactation, severe myelosuppression.
drugs.interactions: Valproic acid, other myelosuppressive agents.
drugs.precautions: Severe hepatic or renal dysfunction, elderly. Males are advised not to father a child during & up to 6 mth after treatment & to seek advice on cryoconservation of sperm prior to treatment because of the possibility of irreversible infertility due to therapy. Patients w/ severe (Grade 3 or 4) vomiting may require antiemetic therapy before initiating Temodal. Monitor FBC. Hepatic injury, including fatal hepatic failure. Baseline liver function tests should be performed prior to treatment initiation. For patients on a 42 day treatment cycle, liver function test should be repeated midway during this cycle. For all patients, liver function test should be checked after each treatment cycle. For patients with significant liver function abnormalities, physicians should assess the benefit/risk of continuing treatment. Liver toxicity may occur several weeks or more after the last treatment of temozolomide.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Temozolomide is a prodrug with active metabolites similar to those produced by dacarbazine.
  • Swallow whole with a glass of water; do not open or chew the capsules.
  • Take on an empty stomach, at least an hour before food.
  • Myelosuppression is dose-limiting effect. Neutrophil nadir occurs about 28 day after treatment, platelet nadir after 26 days. Recovery takes about 2 weeks. Prolonged pancytopenia has occurred and there are rare reports of aplastic anemia.
  • Prophylaxis against PCP is required during combined treatment with temozolomide and radiotherapy.

Lexicomp, 2021

  • Administer consistenly with respect to food (either consistently fasting or nonfasting). Administer on an empty and/or at bedtime to reduce nausea and vomiting.

drugs.indications: Acute myocardial reinfarction where streptokinase is contraindicated due to previous streptokinase induced antibodies. [Indicated when antibodies was given more than 5 days and less than 12 months]
drugs.dosages: Less than 60 kg, 30 mg; 60-69 kg, 35 mg; 70-79 kg, 40 mg; 80-90 kg, 45 mg; 90 kg or above, 50 mg. Administer single IV bolus over 5-10 seconds
drugs.adverseReactions: Nausea, vomiting, hemorrhage, bleeding, epistaxis, GI & GU bleeding, superficial bleeding, reperfusion arrhythmia, hypotension, allergic reaction, fever
drugs.contraindications: Active internal bleeding, hypersensitivity to tenecteplase, history of cerebrovascular accident, intracranial or intraspinal surgery or trauma within 2 months, intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm, known bleeding diathesis, severe uncontrolled hypertension, intracranial aneurysm
drugs.interactions: Drug that affected coagulation and alter platelet function
drugs.precautions: SBP > 180 mmHg, cerebrovascular disease, known/suspected stroke or TIA, recent GI or GUT bleeding, recent IM injection, elderly > 75 years, low body weight < 60 kg
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • The value of thrombolytic drugs for the treatment of myocardial infarction has been established. Streptokinase and alteplase have been shown to reduce mortality. Reteplase and tenecteplase are also licensed for acute myocardial infarction. Thrombolytic drugs are indicated for any patient with acute myocardial infarction for whom the benefit is likely to outweigh the risk of treatment.
  • Alteplase should be given within 6-12 hours of symptom onset, reteplase and streptokinase within 12 hours of symptom onset, but ideally all should be given within 1 hour; use after 12 hours requires specialist advice. Tenecteplase should be given as early as possible and usually within 6 hours of symptom onset.
  • Monitor for intracranial hemorrhage, and monitor blood pressure (antihypertensive recommended if systolic above 180 mmHg or diastolic above 105 mmHg).
  • Serious bleeding calls for discontinuation of the thrombolytic and may require administration of coagulation factors and antifibrinolytic drugs.

British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Chronic hepatitis B (initiated by a specialist)
    • Adult, 25 mg once daily (for duration of treatment, consult product literature).
  • Take with or just after food, or a meal.
  • Manufacturer advises if a dose is more than 18 hours late, the missed dose should not be taken and the next dose should be taken at the normal time.

drugs.indications:
i. Treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults in combination with other antiretroviral agents (such as non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors or protease inhibitors).
ii. Indicated in combination with safer sex practices for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to reduce the risk of sexually acquired HIV-1 infection in adults at high risk.
drugs.prescribingRestrictions:
Indication (ii):
i. To prescribe Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil as part of a comprehensive prevention strategy
ii. All uninfected individuals must be counselled to strictly adhere to the recommended Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil dosing schedule
iii. A negative HIV-1 test must be confirmed immediately prior to initiating Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil. If clinical symptoms consistent with acute viral infection are present and recent (<1 month) exposures are suspected, starting of PrEP must be delayed for at least one month and HIV-1 status need to be reconfirmed, including acute or primary HIV-1 infection; and
iv. To screen HIV-1 infection at least once every 3 months while taking Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Disoproxil for PrEP.
drugs.dosages: 1 tablet once daily.
drugs.adverseReactions: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, flatulence, pain, hypersensitivity, increased pigmentation, asthenia, osteonecrosis, osteomalacia, metabolic abnormalities (e.g. hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperlactatemia), lipodystrophy, elevated lipase, amylase, creatine kinase or transaminases levels, hyperbilirubinemia, insomnia, abnormal dreams, neutropenia, anemia, immune reactivation syndrome, renal impairment, acute renal failure, fanconi syndrome.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to tenofovir or emtricitabine.
drugs.interactions: Increased plasma level of tenofovir and reduced plasma levels of other agent: atazanavir, lopinavir (both have to be co-administered with ritonavir). Increased adverse events of other agent: didanosine. Increased risk of nephrotoxicity when used with other nephrotoxic agents (e.g. aminoglycosides, vancomycin, etc.). Increased plasma level when used with other agents excreted renally by active tubular secretion (e.g. probenecid).
drugs.precautions: Liver impairment; caution in Hepatitis B virus (HBV) coinfection, may result in severe and acute exacerbation or flare up of hepatitis on discontinuation of treatment. Renal impairment; dosing adjustment required in CrCl < 50 ml/min, not recommended if CrCl < 30 ml/min. Avoid co-administration of nephrotoxic agents. Lactation, avoid breast feeding. Avoid co-administration of lamivudine.

Hypophosphatemia, raised amylase and liver enzymes, hepatitis, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperglycemia, neutropenia, nephritis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal impairment, proximal tubulopathy, Fanconi syndrome, immune reconstitution syndrome. Potentially Fatal: Lactic acidosis with severe hepatomegaly with steatosis; severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B. Acute renal failure.
drugs.contraindications: Lactation. Do not co-administer with fixed dose combinations containing tenofovir.
drugs.interactions: Decreased atazanavir concentration with tenofovir unless also co-administered with ritonavir. drugs.precautions: Renal impairment. Hepatomegaly or at risk for liver disease. Elderly and pregnancy. drugs.indications: Indicated for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults

drugs.adverseReactions: Efavirenz (EFV) induced CNS neuropsychiatric manifestations (e.g. headache, disturbance in attention, abnormal dreams, somnolence, insomnia, depression (severe in 1.6%), and anxiety), kidney function decline or failure and bone abnormalities.
drugs.contraindications:
Contraindicated in patients with previously demonstrated hypersensitivity to any of the components of the product. Drugs that are contraindicated or not recommended for use with this fixed-dose combination include:
- Antifungal: voriconazole
- Antimigraine: Ergot derivatives (dihydroergotamine, ergonovine, ergotamine, methylergonovine)
- Benzodiazepines: midazolam, triazolam
- Calcium channel blocker: bepridil
- GI motility agent: cisapride
- Neuroleptic: pimozide
- St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum)
drugs.interactions:
Established and potentially significant drug interactions:
- Protease inhibitor: Atazanavir, Fosamprenavir calcium, Indinavir, Ritonavir, Saquinavir
- CCR5 co-receptor antagonist: Maraviroc
- NRTI: Didanosine
- Anticoagulant: Warfarin
- Anticonvulsants: Carbamazepine, Phenytoin, Phenobarbital
- Antidepressants: Bupropion, Sertraline
- Antifungals: Itraconazole, Ketoconazole, Posaconazole
- Anti-infective: Clarithromycin
- Antimycobacterial: Rifabutin
- Antimycobacterial: Rifampicin
- Calcium channel blockers: Diltiazem, Others (e.g., felodipine, nicardipine, nifedipine, verapamil)
- HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors: Atorvastatin, Pravastatin, Simvastatin
- Hormonal contraceptives: Ethinyl estradiol/Norgestimate, Etonogestrel
- Immunosuppressants: Cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus, and others, metabolized by CYP3A
- Narcotic analgesic: Methadone
drugs.precautions:
- Should be taken cautiously in patients with bone, kidney or liver problems in anamnesis as well as in patients with psychiatric disorders and addictions.
- Particular caution should be exercised in patients coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV. Other more specific precaution include nervous system symptoms, rash, convulsions, immune reconstitution syndrome and fat redistribution.
- Drug should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary, moreover pregnancy should be avoided in women receiving this fixed-dose combination.

drugs.indications:
i) Treatment of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
ii) Hypertension
drugs.dosages:
i) Initial dose: 1 mg at bedtime. Maintenance dose: 5-10 mg once daily.
ii) Initial dose: 1 mg at bedtime. Maintenance dose: 1-5 mg once daily. Max: 20-40 mg/day.
drugs.adverseReactions: Tachycardia, dizziness, syncope, headache and asthenia, nasal congestion, drowsiness, nausea, peripheral edema, postural hypotension.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to terazosin products or other quinazolines
drugs.interactions: In patients currently on beta blockers, the first dose response (marked initial drop in blood pressure, particularly on standing) to an alpha-1 adrenergic blocking drug may be exaggerated. Concomitant therapy with ibuprofen and antihypertensive agents has been reported to result in increases in blood pressure and interference with blood pressure control
drugs.precautions: Carcinoma of the prostate and benign prostatic hyperplasia may cause the same symptoms. Prostate cancer should be ruled out prior to treatment. Dizziness, light-headedness, orthostatic hypotension, syncope (first-dose effect). Patients advised to avoid driving or doing hazardous tasks for the first 12 hours after the initial dose or when dose is increased.
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2022

  • Ureteral stone(s) expulsion (off-label use)
    • Consider for use in patients with ureteral stones >5 and ≤10 mm. Additionally, may consider for use after shock wave lithotripsy to help pass stone fragments.
    • Adult, 2 to 5 mg at bedtime until stone passage or for up to 4 weeks.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2018

  • All selective alpha-blockers appear to be similarly effective for BPH. Silodosin, tamsulosin and alfuzosin have less effect on BP than prazosin or terazosin and may be a better choice for BPH. Dosage titration is required with prazosin and terazosin to minimize hypotensive effects.
  • Dizziness on standing may occur especially when starting treatment or when the dose is increased. Get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimize this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy. Take the first dose at bedtime, but be careful if you get up during the night as you may feel dizzy.
  • This medicine may cause drowsiness or dizziness; do not drive or operate machinery if affected.

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2020

  • Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome is a concern with α-blockers, especially tamsulosin. Men with LUTS being offered α-blockers should be asked about planned cataract surgery. Men with planned cataract surgery should avoid starting α-blockers until their cataract surgery is completed. If already taking an α-blocker, the patient needs to inform his surgeon so that precautions can be taken.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Cream: Adults and children, apply once or twice a day.
    • Tinea corporis, tinea cruris, for 1-2 weeks.
    • Tinea pedis, for 1 week for interdigital type; for 2-4 weeks for plantar/moccasin type.
    • Cutaneous candidiasis, for 1-2 weeks.
  • Gel: Tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea pedis (interdigital), pityriasis versicolor
    • Adults and children, apply once a day for 1 week.

drugs.adverseReactions: Gastrointestinal symptoms, skin reactions, headache, dizziness, vertigo, lymphocytopenia, and visual disturbance. Potentially Fatal: Liver failure, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, neutropenia.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Onychomycosis
    • Adult, 250 mg once daily (6 weeks for fingernails; 12 weeks (sometimes longer) for toenails).
  • Other dermatophyte infection
    • Adult, 250 mg once daily (2-4 weeks for tinea cruris; up to 6 weeks for tinea pedis; 4 weeks for tinea corporis).
  • Renal impairment
    • Adult, CrCl <50 ml/minute (including dialysis), 125 mg once daily.
  • Tell your doctor if you feel unusually tired, nauseous or are not eating; or if you notice dark urine, pale faeces or yellowing of the whites of your eyes or skin; or if you get fever, mouth ulcers, sore throat or unusual bruising.
  • Nail infection: this treatment should cure your nail infection but the nail needs to grow out before it looks completely healthy.
  • Fewer drug interactions than azole antifungals.

Australian Medicines Handbook Children's Dosing Companion, 2021

  • Length of course depends on the infection and its response to treatment.
  • Tinea (except tinea capitis)
    • 1-18 years, use for tinea of the nails, palms, soles, hairy areas (except the scalp), for extensive infection or if topical treatment has failed. Treat for 2-6 weeks (6 weeks for fingernails; 12 weeks for toenails).
    • 10-20 kg, 62.5 mg once daily.
    • 20-40 kg, 125 mg once daily.
    • >40 kg, 250 mg once daily.
  • Tinea capitis
    • 1-18 years, treat for 4-6 weeks.
    • 10-25 kg, 125 mg once daily.
    • 25-35 kg, 187.5 mg once daily.
    • >35 kg, 250 mg once daily.
  • Product information does not include oral doses for children of any age, or topical doses for children <12 years.

  • Manufacturer advises that patients should immediately report any signs or symptoms suggestive of liver dysfunction such as pruritus, unexplained persistent nausea, decreased appetite, anorexia, jaundice, vomiting, fatigue, right upper abdominal pain, dark urine, or pale stools. drugs.indications:
i. Acute oesophageal variceal bleeding.
ii. Treatment of type 1 hepatorenal syndrome, characterised by spontaneous acute renal insufficiency, in patients suffering from severe cirrhosis with ascites.
drugs.dosages:
Indication i: 2 mg IV bolus over 1 minute. Maintenance: 1-2 mg IV bolus 4-6 hourly until bleeding is controlled, up to 24-36 hours. The maximum daily dosage is 120-150 mcg/kg body weight.

Indication ii: Terlipressin is usually started at a dose of 1 mg of terlipressin acetate every 4-6 hours. The dose can be increased to a maximum of 12 mg daily, or 2 mg every 4-6 hours, if serum creatinine levels has not decreased by at least 25% after 3 days of treatment. As an alternative to bolus injection, terlipressin can be administered as a continuous intravenous (IV) infusion with a starting dose of 2 mg of terlipressin acetate/24 hours and increased to a maximum of 12 mg of terlipressin acetate/24 hours.
drugs.adverseReactions: Sepsis/septic shock, hyponatraemia, headache, chest pain, bradycardia, tachycardia, vasoconstriction, peripheral ischemia, pallor, hypertension, cyanosis pulmonary oedema, respiratory distress, respiratory failure, dyspnoea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting.

drugs.indications: Treatment of multiple myeloma.
drugs.dosages: 50 mg to 200 mg daily
drugs.adverseReactions: Severe birth defects, fetal death, drowsiness, somnolence, peripheral neuropathy, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, neutropenia, increase of viral load in HIV-infected patients, hypersensitivity reaction, bradycardia, rash; physical & psychological abuse & dependence. Potentially Fatal: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis and blood dyscrasias.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to thalidomide or to any of the excipients. Pregnancy & lactation. Thalidomide can cause potentially severe birth defects.
drugs.interactions: Thalidomide enhances sedative activity of anxiolytics, hypnotics, antipsychotics, H1 anti-histamines, opiate derivatives, barbiturates and alcohol. Caution when used with beta blockers or anticholinesterase agents. Avoid use of other drugs that have the potential to cause peripheral neuropathy. Increased risk of thromboembolic events with darbepoetin-alfa and doxorubicin.
drugs.precautions: All females of childbearing potential must use 2 reliable forms of contraception simultaneously 4 weeks before starting therapy, during & 4 weeks after therapy is discontinued. For males, use barrier methods of contraception. Do not donate blood or sperm during therapy. Discontinue therapy if any skin rash develops. Patients should be evaluated periodically. Monitor WBC count regularly. May increase risk of venous thromboembolic events. Peripheral neuropathy. History of seizures, Lapp-lactase deficiency/glucose-galactose malabsorption. May impair ability to drive or operate machinery. NPRA Safety Alert (5 June 2017): Risk of viral reactivation and pulmonary hypertension.
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Take at least 1 hour after food and preferably at night to avoid feeling sleepy during the day.
  • You may feel dizzy on standing when taking this medicine. Get up gradually from sitting or lying to minimise this effect; sit or lie down if you become dizzy.
  • Sleepiness and dizziness often occur; avoid driving or using machinery if you are affected.
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy. Thalidomide is a known human teratogen and its analogues, pomalidomide and lenalidomide, are teratogenic in animals.
  • Peripheral neuropathy is related to duration of treatment and cumulative dose although may occur with short-term use; it may be irreversible, particularly if thalidomide is not stopped. May involve sensory, motor or autonomic nerves; symptoms include distal paraesthesia and hyperaesthesia, sensory ataxia, tremor, muscle weakness and cramps. Constipation, bradycardia and orthostatic hypotension may be related to autonomic neuropathy.
  • Risk of VTE with lenalidomide and thalidomide is increased, particularly when combined with other antineoplastics (including dexamethasone). The risk of arterial thromboembolic events (eg MI, stroke, TIA) is also increased. Data with pomalidomide are limited (thromboprophylaxis was used in trials) but it also appears to increase the risk of thromboembolism.

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Patients and their carers should be made aware of the symptoms of thromboembolism and advised to report sudden breathlessness, chest pain, or swelling of a limb.
  • Patients and their carers should be made aware of the symptoms of neutropenia and advised to seek medical advice if symptoms suggestive of neutropenia (such as fever, sore throat) or of thrombocytopenia (such as bleeding) develop.
  • Patients and their carers should be advised to seek medical advice if symptoms of peripheral neuropathy such as paraesthesia, abnormal coordination, or weakness develop.

Other possible reactions include diarrhea, extrasystoles, flushing, hypotension, tachypnoea, potentiation of diuresis, albuminuria, hematuria, rash, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, alopecia, inappropriate ADH secretion(high dose), more serious signs of high serum levels(usually above 30 microgram/mL) such as cardiac arrythmias and convulsions, may appear without prior warning
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to theophylline
drugs.interactions: Azole antifungals, macrolides, quinolones, oral contraceptives, disulfiram, interferon alpha and verapamil, cimetidine, high dose allopurinol
drugs.precautions: Patients with reduced thyroid function, congestive heart failure, acute pulmonary edema, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe hypoxia, pneumonia, acute febrile episodes, viral infection, impaired liver function: reduced theophylline clearance. Patients with cardiac arrythmias, coronary artery disease, unstable angina, cardiomyopathy and severe hypertension. Patients with peptic ulcer disease or gastro esophageal reflux. Concomitant medication use which results in reduced theophylline clearance
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2021

  • Extended release: Administer consistently with or without food (to maintain a consistent drug level); do not chew or crush tablets; may split tablet if scored. An intact matrix tablet may pass in stool.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • This medicine interacts with many other drugs; ask your doctor or pharmacist before using any other medicines including herbal and over-the-counter products.

British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Therapeutic monitoring:
    • In most individuals, a plasma-theophylline concentration of 10-20 mg/litre (55-110 micromol/litre) is required for satisfactory bronchodilation, although a lower plasma-theophylline concentration of 5-15 mg/litre may be effective. Adverse effects can occur within the range 10-20 mg/litre and both the frequency and severity increase at concentrations above 20 mg/litre.
    • Plasma-theophylline concentration is measured 5 days after starting oral treatment and at least 3 days after any dose adjustment. A blood sample should usually be taken 4-6 hours after an oral dose of a modified-release preparation (sampling times may vary: consult local guidelines).
  • Smoking can increase theophylline clearance and increased doses of theophylline are therefore required; dose adjustments are likely to be necessary if smoking started or stopped during treatment.
  • Theophylline in overdose can cause vomiting (which may be severe and intractable), agitation, restlessness, dilated pupils, sinus tachycardia, and hyperglycaemia. More serious effects are haematemesis, convulsions, and supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias. Severe hypokalaemia may develop rapidly.
  • Potentially serious hypokalaemia may result from beta2 agonist therapy. Particular caution is required in severe asthma, because this effect may be potentiated by concomitant treatment with theophylline and its derivatives, corticosteroids, and diuretics, and by hypoxia. Plasma-potassium concentration should therefore be monitored in severe asthma.

Martindale The Complete Drug Reference, 2020

  • Thiamazole is a thiourea antithyroid drug that acts by blocking the production of thyroid hormones. It is used in the management of hyperthyroidism, including the treatment of Graves' disease, in the preparation of hyperthyroid patients for thyroidectomy, as an adjunct to radio-iodine therapy, and in the treatment of thyroid storm.
  • Thiamazole is given orally usually in an initial dosage of 15 to 60 mg daily. It is usually given in three divided doses but single daily doses have also been used. When the patient is euthyroid the dose is gradually reduced to a maintenance dose, usually 5 to 15 mg daily. Maintenance treatment is usually continued for 1 to 2 years, although the optimum duration has not been established.
  • Thiamazole has also been used with supplemental levothyroxine as a blocking-replacement regimen.
  • The initial oral dose of thiamazole for hyperthyroidism in children is 400 micrograms/kg daily, in 3 divided doses; the maintenance dose may be half of this.

drugs.indications: Thyrogen (thyrotropin alfa) is indicated for use as an adjunctive treatment for radioiodine ablation of thyroid tissue remnants in patients who have undergone a near-total or total thyroidectomy for well-differentiated thyroid cancer and who do not have evidence of distant metastatic thyroid cancer.
drugs.dosages: A two-injection regimen is recommended for thyrotropin administration. The two-injection regimen is thyrotropin 0.9 mg intramuscularly (IM), followed by a second 0.9 mg IM injection 24 hours later. After reconstitution with 1.2 ml Sterile Water for Injection, 1.0 ml solution (0.9 mg thyrotropin alfa) is administered by intramuscular injection to the buttock. For radioiodine imaging or treatment, radioiodine administration should be given 24 hours following the final Thyrogen injection. Diagnostic scanning should be performed 48 hours after radioiodine administration, whereas post-therapy scanning may be delayed additional days to allow background activity to decline.
drugs.adverseReactions: Nausea, headache, fatigue, vomiting, dizziness, paresthesia, asthenia, diarrhea. Thyrogen administration may cause transient (< 48 hours) influenza-like symptoms [also called flu-like symptoms (FLS)], which may include fever (>100°F/38°C), chills/shivering, myalgia/arthralgia, fatigue/asthenia/ malaise, headache (non-focal), chills.
drugs.contraindications: None
drugs.interactions: Formal interaction studies between Thyrogen and other medicinal products have not been performed.
drugs.precautions: Do not inject IV. Patients previously treated with bovine TSH. Renal impairment. High-risk elderly patients with functioning thyroid tumors &/or patients with heart disease. Pregnancy & lactation.

drugs.indications:
i. Treatment of complaints resulting from the natural or surgical menopause & in cases at high risk for breast carcinomas where general hormone replacement therapy is contraindicated.
ii. Prevention of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of future fractures who are intolerant of, or contraindicated for, other medicinal products approved for the prevention of osteoporosis.
drugs.dosages: 2.5 mg daily
drugs.adverseReactions: Endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma (rare), change in body weight, vaginal bleeding, gastrointestinal upsets, changes in liver parameters, increased facial hair growth, pretibial edema and arthralgia or myalgia.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to tibolone, breast cancer (known or suspected), estrogen-dependent neoplasms, cerebrovascular disease, history of stroke, arterial disease, thromboembolic disorders, history of cholestatic jaundice, hepatic tumors (benign or malignant), abnormal vaginal bleeding
drugs.interactions: Enhances the effect of anticoagulants such as warfarin since Tibolone can increase blood fibrinolytic activity. Concurrent administration of tibolone and tacrolimus may lead to increased tacrolimus toxicity
drugs.precautions: Women with hormone dependent tumors, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disorders including thrombophlebitis, thromboembolic processes or a history of these conditions, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding and severe liver disorders. Liver disease. Patients with hypercholesterolemia and impaired glucose tolerance. Stop tibolone 4 weeks before elective surgery when prolonged immobilization after surgery is likely
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) with small doses of an oestrogen (together with a progestogen in women with a uterus) is appropriate for alleviating menopausal symptoms such as vaginal atrophy or vasomotor instability. Oestrogen given systemically in the perimenopausal and postmenopausal period or tibolone given in the postmenopausal period also diminish postmenopausal osteoporosis but other drugs are preferred. Menopausal atrophic vaginitis may respond to a short course of a topical vaginal oestrogen preparation used for a few weeks and repeated if necessary.
  • Tibolone combines oestrogenic and progestogenic activity with weak androgenic activity; it is given continuously, without cyclical progestogen.
  • HRT increases the risk of venous thromboembolism, stroke, endometrial cancer (reduced by a progestogen), breast cancer, and ovarian cancer; there is an increased risk of coronary heart disease in women who start combined HRT more than 10 years after menopause.
  • The MHRA advises that HRT should only be prescribed to relieve post-menopausal symptoms that are adversely affecting quality of life and treatment should be reviewed regularly to ensure the minimum effective dose is used for the shortest duration. For osteoporosis, consider alternative treatments. HRT does not prevent coronary heart disease or protect against a decline in cognitive function and it should not be prescribed for these purposes. Experience of treating women over 65 years with HRT is limited.

drugs.brandName: Brilinta, Reclovac, Supagrel, Tgson, Thinhet, Ticalet
drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Prevention of atherothrombotic events in patients with a history of myocardial infarction and a high risk of an atherothrombotic event [in combination with aspirin]
    • Adult, 60 mg twice daily, extended treatment may be started without interruption after the initial 12-month therapy for acute coronary syndrome. Treatment may also be initiated up to 2 years from the myocardial infarction, or within 1 year after stopping previous ADP receptor inhibitor treatment. There are limited data on the efficacy and safety of extended treatment beyond 3 years.

Surviving Prescribing A Practical Guide, 2020

  • Ticagrelor has a more rapid onset of antiplatelet activity than clopidogrel. It is associated with lower rates of death, non-fatal MI or stroke after an initial ACS episode (PLATO trial), but with higher rates of intracranial and GI bleeding, and premature discontinuation.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • The active metabolite of the thienopyridines (clopidogrel, prasugrel) irreversibly binds to the platelet P2Y12 receptor and inhibits platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet. Ticagrelor binds reversibly to the P2Y12
  • Avoid grapefruit juice as it may increase the risk of bleeding.
  • Dyspnoea is not usually severe, occurs in the first few weeks of treatment and, although it sometimes leads to discontinuation, it does not appear to be associated with worsening respiratory or cardiac disease (it may be related to a ticagrelor-induced increase in adenosine levels).
  • Surgery
    • Weigh risk of cardiovascular events (including stent thrombosis) from stopping antiplatelet agents against bleeding risk if continued; it may be safe to continue antiplatelet agents before minor surgery with low risk of bleeding, e.g. dental procedures, cataract surgery or some dermatological procedures.
    • It may be necessary to reduce the antiplatelet effect before surgery with a high bleeding risk, e.g. CABG.
    • For patients with coronary stents, consider delaying elective surgery until dual antiplatelet treatment is no longer required; consult patient's cardiologist before stopping antiplatelet agents.
    • If antiplatelet effect is not wanted, stop clopidogrel >5 days before, prasugrel >7 days before and ticagrelor 5 days before planned surgery.

i) Prevention of thrombotic stroke for patients who are sensitive /intolerant to Acetylsalicylic Acid
ii) Maintenance of coronary bypass surgery or angioplasty
iii) Maintenance of patency of access in patients on chronic hemodialysis
drugs.dosages: 250 mg twice daily taken with food
drugs.adverseReactions: Minor gastrointestinal disorders. Rarely cutaneous allergic manifestations, thrombocytopenia, cholestatic icterus and or rise in transaminases. Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (monitor full blood count weekly initially)
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ticlopidine or its components, patients with active bleeding disorders. Neutropenia or thrombocytopenia, severe liver impairment
drugs.interactions: Any drugs likely to produce coagulation
drugs.precautions: Predisposition to bleeding, including gastric or duodenal ulcers. Underlying hematologic disorders. Concomitant oral anticoagulant therapy or nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents (including aspirin). Liver disease, patients undergoing lumbar puncture or surgical procedure. Ticlopidine should be discontinued if the absolute neutrophil count falls below 1200/mm3 or if the platelet count falls below 80,000/mm3. If possible, ticlopidine should be discontinued 10 to 14 days prior to surgery
drugs.notes:
Rang and Dale's Pharmacology, 2020

  • Ticlopidine was the first adenosine (P2Y12) receptor antagonist to be introduced, but causes neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The main agents are currently clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor, each of which is combined with low-dose aspirin in patients with unstable coronary artery disease, usually for up to 1 year.

Lexicomp, 2020

  • Administer with food. Ticlopidine bioavailability may be increased (20%) if taken with food.
  • Due to its association with life-threatening hematologic disorders, ticlopidine should be reserved for patients who are intolerant to aspirin, who have failed aspirin therapy, or who are not eligible to receive other antiplatelet therapy.
  • May cause life-threatening hematologic reactions, including neutropenia, agranulocytosis, thrombotic thrombocytopenia purpura (TTP), and aplastic anemia. Routine monitoring is required. Monitor for signs and symptoms of neutropenia including WBC count. Discontinue if the absolute neutrophil count falls to <1200/mm3 or if laboratory signs of TTP or aplastic anemia occur.

drugs.notes:
Product leaflet, accessed 2020 - Nutriva

  • Traditionally used for relief of cough, cold and sinusitis.
    • Adults, take 1-2 capsules daily after a meal.

The Review of Natural Products, 2020

  • Tibetan history records the first uses of yartsa gunbu in the 15th century. Cordyceps is considered to be derived from the Latin cord (club), ceps (head), and sinesis (from China). The fruiting body and attached mycelium of cordyceps have been used in Chinese culture and in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries. drugs.brandName: Timoptol, Iotim, Optimol, Optimolol, Timo-comod, Timolain
drugs.indications: Elevated intraocular pressure, chronic open angle glaucoma
drugs.dosages: One drop in the affected eye(s) twice daily or as directed by physician
drugs.adverseReactions: Bradycardia, hypotension, confusion, depression, dizziness, fatigue, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, dry eye, ocular burning, corneal anesthesia
drugs.contraindications: Bronchial asthma or a history of bronchial asthma, severe COPD, sinus bradycardia, second or third degree atrioventricular block, overt cardiac failure and cardiogenic shock
drugs.interactions: Catecholamine-depleting drugs. Concurrent administration of oral or systemic beta-adrenergic blockers. Concurrent use of beta-blockers and digitalis with diltiazem or verapamil may have additive effects in prolonging atrioventricular conduction time. Quinidine
drugs.precautions: History of atopy or a history of severe anaphylactic reaction to a variety of allergens, pregnancy and lactation. May impair ability to drive or operate machinery
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2020

  • Elevated intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma, adult
    • Gel-forming solution: instill 1 drop (either 0.25% or 0.5% solution) once daily.
    • Solution: initially instill 1 drop (0.25% solution) into affected eye(s) twice daily; if response is not adequate, increase to 1 drop (0.5% solution) twice daily. May decrease dose to 1 drop once daily if intraocular pressure is well controlled.
  • Infantile hemangioma, superficial
    • Limited data available: Infants and Children: Topical: Gel-forming solution: Apply 1 drop of the 0.5% gel-forming solution twice daily to the site.
    • The largest experience is a multicenter retrospective report describing use in over 60 patients which showed improvement in all but one patient with a mean duration of treatment of 3.4 ± 2.7 months.
    • A smaller, randomized trial compared timolol 0.5% gel (n=15) to placebo (n=17) on superficial infantile lesions covering various areas of the body; initial lesion improvements were observed after 12 to 16 weeks, and significant color changes reported at week 24.
    • A smaller (n=13) retrospective, open-label trial also showed success with two drops of 0.25% timolol gel-forming solution twice daily on periocular infantile hemangiomas.
    • Timolol was reported as being well tolerated in the trials.

Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Timolol is a nonselective beta1 and beta2 receptor blocker whereas betaxolol selectively blocks beta1 receptors. Although studies suggest betaxolol is less likely to cause bronchospasm than timolol, it should be used with caution in patients with asthma.
  • Betaxolol may be less effective at reducing intraocular pressure and is more likely to cause local stinging compared to timolol.

Product Leaflet, accessed 2022

  • Iotim: Use the solution within 1 month after opening the vial.
  • Timo-Comod: To be used within 12 weeks after opening.
  • Timoptol-XE: Discard 1 month after opening.

drugs.genericName: Tinzaparin Sodium 10,000 anti-Factor Xa IU/ml Injection in Prefilled Syringe/Cartridge
drugs.prescriberCategory: DELISTED FROM MOHMF 2020-1 because product withdrawal from market since 2019, alternatives are preferred since more prominent studies available, only used for DVT in pregnant women and rarely used in cardiology setting.
drugs.indications:
i) Treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), not amounting to hemodynamic instability.
ii) Prevention of post-operative DVT in patients undergoing general and orthopedic surgery.
drugs.dosages:
i) Treatment of DVT and PE, in conjunction with warfarin: 175 anti-Factor Xa IU/kg SC once daily for at least 6 days.
ii) Thromboprophylaxis in patients with:
Moderate risk of thrombosis (general surgery), 3,500 anti-Factor Xa IU SC 2 hrs before surgery and postoperatively, 3,500 anti-Factor Xa IU once daily for 7-10 days.
High risk of thrombosis (e.g. total hip replacement), 4,500 anti-Factor Xa IU SC or 50 anti-Factor Xa IU/kg body weight SC 2 hrs before surgery and then once daily until the patients has been mobilized.
drugs.adverseReactions: Skin necrosis, erythema, increased liver function test, local pain, major bleeding, granulocytopenic disorder (rare), hematoma, neurological injury with concurrent use of spinal or epidural anesthesia, pancytopenia, thrombocytopenia anaphylaxis, priapism and death.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to sodium bisulfite, treatment of DVT in patient 90 years old and older with renal insufficiency, generalized or local hemorrhagic tendency, uncontrolled severe hypertension, acute cerebral insults, septic endocarditis.
drugs.interactions: Salicylates, NSAIDs, vitamin K antagonists, dextran.
drugs.precautions: Renal or hepatic impairment, recent cerebral hemorrhage, trauma, recent surgery to the central nervous system, concurrent spinal or epidural anesthesia, bleeding disorders, severe thrombocytopenia. Do not administer IM (risk of hematoma).
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2024

  • Administration: Subcutaneous
    • Patient should be lying down or sitting. Administer by deep SubQ injection into the lower abdomen (avoding navel area), outer thigh, lower back or upper arm. Do not administer IM. Injection site should be varied daily. To minimize bruising, do not rub the injection site.

British National Formulary 88, 2024

  • Routine monitoring of anti-Factor Xa activity is not usually required during treatment with tinzaparin, but may be necessary in patients at increased risk of bleeding (e.g. in renal impairment and those who are underweight or overweight).

drugs.adverseReactions: Bleeding manifestations, reversible thrombocytopenia, nausea, fever, headache
drugs.contraindications: Abnormal bleeding within 30 days, stroke within 30 days or any history of hemorrhagic stroke, intracranial disease (aneurysm, neoplasm or arteriovenous malformation), severe hypertension, hemorrhagic diathesis, increased prothrombin time or INR, thrombocytopenia and breast-feeding
drugs.interactions: Drugs that affect hemostasis (e.g. warfarin)
drugs.precautions: Renal impairment, hepatic impairment, major surgery or severe trauma within 3 months, traumatic or protracted cardiopulmonary resuscitation, organ biopsy, recent bleeding including history of gastrointestinal bleeding or genitourinary bleeding, platelet disorder or history of thrombocytopenia; platelet count <150,000 cells/mm3
drugs.notes:
Sarawak Handbook of Medical Emergencies, 2019

  • Platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists are not widely available due to cost.
  • Three intravenous GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists approved for clinical use
    • Abciximab (Reopro)
    • Eptifibatide (Integrilin)
    • Tirofiban (Aggrastat)

ACCP Updates in Therapeutics, 2021

  • GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors reduce the incidence of composite ischemic events, primarily through decreasing documented MIs, but can increase the risk of bleeding.
  • Benefit from adding GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors to aspirin therapy is greatest among those with highest-risk features (elevated biomarkers, diabetes, undergoing revascularization) and in those not receiving adequate pretreatment with clopidogrel or ticagrelor.
  • Most common adverse effect is bleeding, with rates as low as 1.4% and as high as 10.6%, depending on length of therapy and how bleeding rates were accrued in the individual studies.
  • All GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors can cause thrombocytopenia; monitor hemoglobin (Hgb), hematocrit (Hct), and platelets.
  • Secondary to their short half-life, eptifibatide and tirofiban can be reversed within a few hours by discontinuing the infusion and are preferred options in NSTE-ACS guideline.

drugs.genericName: Tirzepatide 10 mg per dose Solution for Injection in Pre-filled Pen
drugs.indications:
Weight management: As an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for weight management, including weight loss and weight maintenance, in adults with an initial Body Mass Index (BMI) of:
i. ≥30 kg/m2 (obesity) or
ii. ≥27 kg/m2 to <30 kg/m2 (overweight) in the presence of at least one weight-related comorbid condition (e.g., hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiovascular disease, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes mellitus).
drugs.prescribingRestrictions:
i. Adults above 18 years old with T2DM, BMI ≥32.5 kg/m2 who had:

  • Failed lifestyle intervention AND
  • Failed one GLP-1 receptor agonist for T2DM

OR
Adults above 18 years old with BMI≥37.5 kg/m2 who had:

  • Failed lifestyle intervention AND
  • With at least one obesity-related comorbidity [obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), heart failure (HF), chronic kidney disease (CKD) or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH)]

ii. To be prescribed by Endocrinologists only.
drugs.dosages: Initiate tirzepatide at 2.5 mg weekly for 4 weeks, then increase to 5 mg weekly. If clinically required, escalate in 2.5 mg increments at minimum 4-week intervals to recommended maintenance doses of 5 mg, 10 mg, or a maximum of 15 mg weekly.
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypersensitivity reactions, hypoglycaemia, dizziness, hypotension, nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, dyspepsia, abdominal distention, eructation, flatulence, gastrooesophageal reflux disease, hair loss, fatigue, injection site reactions, heart rate increased, lipase increased, amylase increased, blood calcitonin increased, dysgeusia, cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, and acute pancreatitis.
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to tirzepatide or to any of the excipients (disodium hydrogen phosphate heptahydrate, benzyl alcohol, glycerol, phenol, sodium chloride, concentrated hydrochloric acid, sodium hydroxide and water for injections).
drugs.interactions: None
drugs.precautions: Acute pancreatitis, hypoglycaemia, gastrointestinal effects, severe gastrointestinal disease, diabetic retinopathy and aspiration in association with general anaesthesia or deep sedation. NPRA Safety Alert (22 July 2026): Risk of Severe Acute Pancreatitis. NPRA Safety Alert (13 Oct 2026): Risk of Intestinal Obstruction.
drugs.notes:
Lexicomp, 2024

  • Diabetes mellitus, Type 2, treatment
    • Adult, by subcutaneous injection, initial: 2.5 mg once weekly for 4 weeks, then increase to 5 mg once weekly. May increase dose in 2.5 mg/week increments every 4 weeks if needed to achieve glycemic goals (maximum weekly dose: 15 mg/week).
    • The lower initial dose (2.5 mg weekly) is intended to reduce GI symptoms; it does not provide effective glycemic control. If changing the day of administration is necessary, allow at least 72 hours between 2 doses.
    • Due to lack of additive glycemic benefit, avoid concomitant use with a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor.
  • Weight management, chronic
    • For use as an adjunct to diet and exercise in patients with a BMI ≥30 kg/m2 or patients with a BMI ≥27 kg/m2 and ≥1 weight-associated comorbidity (e.g., cardiovascular disease, dyslipidemia, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, type 2 diabetes mellitus).
    • Adult, by subcutaneous injection, initial: 2.5 mg once weekly for 4 weeks, then increase to 5 mg once weekly. May further increase dose in 2.5 mg/week increments every 4 weeks, if needed (maximum weekly dose: 15 mg/week).
    • The lower initial dose (2.5 mg weekly) is intended to reduce GI symptoms; it does not provide effective weight loss. If changing the day of administration is necessary, allow at least 72 hours between 2 doses.
  • Missed dose should be administered as soon as possible within 4 days; resume usual schedule thereafter. If >4 days have elapsed, skip the missed dose and resume administration at the next scheduled weekly dose.
  • In both male and female rats, tirzepatide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell tumors at clinically relevant exposures. It is unknown whether tirzepatide causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans as human relevance of tirzepatide-induced rodent thyroid C-cell tumors has not been determined.
  • Store at 2-8°C. If needed, each single-dose pen can be stored unrefrigerated at temperatures ≤30°C for up to 21 days; do not return to the refrigerator and discard if not used within 21 days. Do not freeze or use if frozen. Store in the original carton to protect from light.

drugs.notes:
British National Formulary 82, 2021

  • Spasticity associated with multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury or disease
    • Adult, initially 2 mg daily, then increased in steps of 2 mg daily in divided doses, increased at intervals of at least 3-4 days and adjust according to response; usual dose up to 24 mg daily in 3-4 divided doses; maximum 36 mg per day.
  • Avoid abrupt withdrawal (risk of rebound hypertension and tachycardia); to minimize risk, discontinue gradually and monitor blood pressure.
  • Drowsiness may affect performance of skilled tasks (e.g. driving); effects of alcohol enhanced.
  • Monitor liver function monthly for first 4 months for daily doses of 12 mg or higher, and in those who develop unexplained nausea, anorexia or fatigue.

MIMS, 2021

  • Steroid-responsive inflammatory ocular condition for which corticosteroid is indicated & where superficial bacterial ocular infection or risk of bacterial ocular infection exists.
    • Ophthalmic suspension, 1-2 drops into conjunctival sac every 4-6 hours, may be increased to 1-2 drops every 2 hours during initial 24-48 hours.
    • Ophthalmic ointment, apply ½ inch ribbon into conjunctival sac up to TDS-QDS. May be used at bedtime in conjunction with ophthalmic drops.

  • Discard 4 weeks after opening.

drugs.genericName: Tocilizumab 162 mg/0.9 ml Solution for Injection in Prefilled Syringe (for Subcutaneous Injection)
drugs.indications:
Indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe active rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in adult patients:
i) with inadequate respond or intolerance to conventional disease- modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDS)
ii) who has failed antitumor necrosis factors (antiTNFs)
iii) where TNF is contraindicated (patients with history of pulmonary tuberculosis [PTB])

It also can be used as monotherapy or with combination with methotrexate (MTX) and/ or other DMARDS.
drugs.dosages: Adult patients, 162 mg given once every week as a subcutaneous injection.
drugs.adverseReactions: Hypertension, rash, diarrhea, upper abdominal pain, ALT/SGPT level raised, dizziness, headache, nasopharyngitis, injection site reaction, gastrointestinal perforation, decreased platelet count, neutropenia, anaphylaxis, hypersensitivity reaction, upper respiratory infection
drugs.contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to tocilizumab and patients with a concurrent serious infection
drugs.interactions: CYP450 enzymes, simvastatin, atorvastatin, ca-channel blockers, theophylline, warfarin, phenytoin, ciclosporin, benzodiazepines
drugs.precautions: Should not be initiated in patients with active infections. Complications of diverticulitis. Tuberculosis, vaccinations, hypersensitivity reactions, active hepatic disease and hepatic impairment, viral reactivation, demyelinating disorders
drugs.notes:
Australian Medicines Handbook, 2021

  • Tell your doctor or nurse immediately if you have difficulty breathing, a rash or feel faint. This is most likely to happen during, or within an hour of, the IV infusion.
  • Contact your doctor urgently if you develop abdominal pain, symptoms of an allergy or persistent fever or other signs of an infection.
  • Consider need for immunization before starting treatment (live vaccines should not be given during treatment).

British National Formulary 81, 2021

  • Manufacturer advises discontinue if absolute neutrophil count less than 0.5 x 109/litre or platelet count less than 50 x 103/microlitre).
  • Manufacturer advises caution if hepatic enzymes more than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal and discontinue if hepatic enzymes more than 5 times the upper limit of normal.

MIMS, 2022

  • Store the prefilled syringe in a refrigerator at a temperature of 2-8°C. Do not freeze, keep in carton to protect from light, and keep dry.
